guides.title: The Metre: Definition, History and Realisation
guides.summary: The metre is the world's agreed unit of length, and this guide traces how it was invented, redefined four times, and is physically produced in laboratories today. It covers the meridian survey, the platinum prototype bars, the krypton wavelength era, the fixed speed of light, laser interferometry, calibration chains and the practical limits of measuring length.

sections.heading: Why a unit of length has to be manufactured
sections.body:
Every measurement is a comparison. When someone says a beam is 4.2 metres long, they are asserting that the beam, laid end to end against some agreed reference thing, matches it 4.2 times over. All of engineering, trade, navigation, surveying and experimental physics rests on the quiet assumption that the agreed reference thing is identical for everyone, everywhere, and does not drift with time. That assumption is not a gift of nature. It has to be built, maintained, distributed and continually re-checked by an international apparatus of national laboratories, and the history of how humanity constructed that apparatus for length is the history of the metre.

The difficulty is much greater than it first appears. Suppose you settle the matter by machining a bar of metal and declaring it to be one unit long. You immediately inherit four problems. The bar expands and contracts with temperature: ordinary carbon steel changes length by roughly 11 parts in a million for every kelvin, so a one-metre steel rule that warms by 5 °C grows by about 55 micrometres, which is more than half the thickness of a human hair and catastrophic in precision work. The bar corrodes, creeps under its own weight and slowly relaxes internal stresses left from manufacture, so its length changes by small amounts over decades in ways nobody can predict. The bar can be destroyed by fire, war or accident, and if it is unique its destruction destroys the unit. And the bar exists in one place, whereas measurement happens everywhere, so copies must be made, and every copy introduces error that accumulates down the chain.

Modern demands make these problems acute rather than academic. Semiconductor lithography now patterns features a few nanometres across, and the machines that make them must position stages to sub-nanometre repeatability. Satellite navigation depends on distances between orbiting clocks and ground stations being modelled to centimetres over twenty thousand kilometres. The LIGO gravitational-wave detectors sense changes in a four-kilometre arm of about 10 to the minus 19 metres, roughly one ten-thousandth the width of a proton. At the other end, a machinist fitting a bearing to an interference fit needs a shaft diameter correct to two or three micrometres, and a mismatch of ten micrometres between his micrometer and the bearing-maker's is the difference between a working assembly and scrap.

What unites all of these is that people who have never met, working on different continents and in different decades, must agree about length to a stated tolerance and be able to prove that agreement. That proof is what a unit definition, and the machinery for realising it, exists to supply. The metre is not a stick; it is a social and technical contract about how to answer the question "how long is that", enforced by measurable evidence.

sections.heading: Before the metre: the tangle of local measures
sections.body:
For most of recorded history, length was local, anthropometric and legally fragmented. Units were derived from the body — the cubit as the forearm from elbow to fingertip, the foot, the span of a hand, the fathom as the reach of outstretched arms, the pace — because bodies were the only measuring instruments universally available. Egyptian royal cubit rods of about 523 millimetres, cut in wood or stone and issued as standards to be checked against a granite master, survive from the third millennium BC and show that the problem of maintaining a standard was understood at least four and a half thousand years ago. The Roman pes of roughly 296 millimetres, the Mesopotamian kush, the Chinese chi and the Indian angula all served the same function within their spheres.

The trouble was that they did not agree, and the disagreement was not merely between civilisations but within them. In eighteenth-century France, the standard historical estimate is that a quarter of a million distinct units of weights and measures were in local use, with names repeating from town to town but values differing. A pied du roi in Paris was 324.8 millimetres, but a "foot" in a Provençal market town might be several percent different, and the aune used for cloth varied from roughly 1.19 metres to over 1.4 metres depending on the region and whether it was measuring linen, wool or silk. Because the local lord frequently controlled the standard, and because rents and tithes were often paid in measured goods, a quiet enlargement of the grain measure was a mechanism for extracting more from tenants. Peasant grievance lists compiled before the French Revolution — the cahiers de doléances of 1789 — repeatedly demanded "one king, one law, one weight and one measure", which tells you that the metrological complaint was political before it was scientific.

England was somewhat better organised, having enforced statute standards since at least Magna Carta and having fixed the yard by royal exchequer bars, but even there the definitions were circular and the artefacts inconsistent. The British yard was defined by a bronze bar; when the Houses of Parliament burned in 1834 the primary imperial standard yard was damaged, and the replacement had to be reconstructed by comparison with surviving secondary copies, a laborious project completed only in 1855. That episode is the clearest possible illustration of why depending on a single object is dangerous.

Two forces finally broke the deadlock. Trade across borders grew to the point where conversion tables became a genuine tax on commerce, and science began to demand precision that local custom could not supply. Astronomers comparing measurements of the Earth's shape, engineers building steam machinery to fits of a hundredth of an inch, and chemists weighing reagents all needed a common language of quantity. The metre was born of that convergence: a political revolution that wanted uniformity, and a scientific community that wanted reproducibility.

sections.heading: The meridian survey and the birth of the metre, 1791 to 1799
sections.body:
In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences, asked by the National Assembly to devise a rational system of measures, made a decision of enormous consequence: the new unit of length would not be tied to a king's body or an existing bar, but derived from the Earth itself. The metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator along the meridian passing through Paris. The reasoning was ideological as much as practical — a unit taken from the planet belonged to everyone and to no monarch, "à tous les temps, à tous les peuples", for all times and all peoples — but it also had a scientific appeal, because the Earth was believed to be a stable object that any future civilisation could re-measure.

The Academy also considered defining the unit by the length of a pendulum beating seconds, which is about 994 millimetres at Paris latitude and is far easier to reproduce. It was rejected chiefly because the pendulum's period depends on local gravity, which varies with latitude and altitude, so the unit would have had to be tied to a particular place and would have entangled length with the definition of the second. That objection was sound, and it prefigures a theme that recurs through the whole subject: a good definition should depend on as few other quantities as possible.

Realising the Earth-based definition required measuring an arc of the meridian. Two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre working south from Dunkirk and Pierre Méchain working north from Barcelona, were despatched in 1792 to survey the arc by triangulation — measuring the angles of a chain of triangles between hilltops and church towers, with two carefully measured baselines near Melun and Perpignan to set the scale. The work took six years instead of the planned one, conducted through the Terror and a war with Spain. Both men were arrested at various points as suspicious characters carrying strange instruments; Méchain was detained in Spain and could not return.

The survey's most famous problem was Méchain's discovery of an inconsistency of a few seconds of arc in his latitude determinations at Barcelona, which he concealed and agonised over until his death of malaria in 1804 while attempting to extend the survey. The historian Ken Alder's reconstruction of the affair argues persuasively that Méchain's error was real but unremarkable, and that his concealment of it mattered more to metrology's culture than to its numbers, because it forced later practitioners to confront the idea that all measurements carry uncertainty which must be declared rather than hidden. The resulting metre was short of its intended value by about 0.2 millimetres, largely because the flattening of the Earth used in the calculation was slightly wrong. The definition was aspirational; the artefact that came out of it became the real standard.

sections.heading: The Mètre des Archives and the first metric system
sections.body:
On 22 June 1799 two platinum artefacts were deposited in the French national archives: a bar defining the metre and a cylinder defining the kilogram. The bar, known ever after as the Mètre des Archives, was a flat rectangular section of platinum roughly 25 millimetres wide and 4 millimetres thick, and it was an end standard — the unit was the distance between its two polished end faces, not marks engraved on it. It measured 443.296 lignes of the old French toise, a conversion recorded so that the new unit could be tied to the old measurements which the survey had actually produced.

The choice of an end standard mattered. To use it you must bring another object into contact with both ends, or wring a probe against each face, and every contact deforms the surfaces slightly and wears them over decades. Any dirt on an end face adds directly to the measured length. End standards are convenient for comparing to gauge blocks and awkward for optical comparison, and the accumulated wear of a century of use is one reason the artefact was eventually replaced rather than merely re-certified.

Around the metre a whole system was constructed on two principles that still govern the SI. The first was decimal scaling: multiples and submultiples by powers of ten, with Greek prefixes for multiples — deca, hecto, kilo — and Latin ones for submultiples — deci, centi, milli. This eliminated the mental arithmetic of twelve inches to a foot and three feet to a yard, and made unit conversion a matter of moving a decimal point. The second was coherence: derived units built from base units with no numerical conversion factors. Area is the square metre, volume the cubic metre; the litre was fixed as a cubic decimetre, and the gram as the mass of a cubic centimetre of water at its temperature of maximum density, about 4 °C. That linkage of length to mass through water was elegant, and it silently made the kilogram depend on the metre, on the purity of water and on a temperature scale — an entanglement later generations spent great effort undoing.

Adoption was slow and politically contested. The metric system was made compulsory in France in 1795, effectively suspended under Napoleon in 1812 in favour of "mesures usuelles" that dressed the old names over metric quantities, and only made definitively obligatory again in 1840. Ordinary people resisted units that had no relation to the hand, the arm or the customary sack. What eventually carried the system was not decree but utility: scientists adopted it because calculations were easier, and international trade adopted it because a common system beat a thicket of conversions. By the 1860s the metre was in use well beyond France, and the pressure to formalise its custody internationally had become irresistible.

sections.heading: The Metre Convention of 1875 and the international prototype
sections.body:
On 20 May 1875 seventeen states signed the Convention du Mètre in Paris, an international treaty that remains the legal foundation of the modern measurement system. It created three permanent bodies whose names are worth knowing because they still issue the definitions in force: the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), a diplomatic assembly of member states that meets roughly every four years and votes on definitions; the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM), a smaller body of scientists that governs between conferences; and the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), a laboratory at Sèvres near Paris, sited on internationally administered ground, which holds the standards and does the comparison work. The anniversary of the signing is now observed as World Metrology Day.

The Convention's first great technical project was a new metre. Thirty bars were cast from an alloy of 90 percent platinum and 10 percent iridium, chosen because it is extremely hard, chemically inert, takes a fine polish and has a low coefficient of thermal expansion of about 8.7 parts per million per kelvin. Crucially, the bars were given a Tresca cross-section: an X-shaped profile, like a capital H with the crossbar in the middle, about 20 millimetres across. That shape places most of the metal far from the neutral axis, which makes the bar very stiff in bending for its weight, so it sags less under gravity and its neutral plane — the surface that neither stretches nor compresses when the bar flexes — lies exactly where the defining lines are engraved.

The bars were line standards, not end standards. Three fine lines were ruled at each end of the central web, and the metre was the distance between the middle line at one end and the middle line at the other, measured with a microscope. Line standards can be read optically without touching the artefact, which removes wear and contamination from routine use — a direct lesson from the Mètre des Archives.

The definition adopted by the first CGPM in 1889 specified conditions with new care: the metre was the distance between the axes of the two central lines on the international prototype at the temperature of melting ice, with the bar supported on two rollers at least one centimetre in diameter placed symmetrically 571 millimetres apart. Those support points are the Airy points, the positions that minimise the change in length between the end faces due to bending; specifying them was an admission that the artefact's length depends on how you hold it.

Bar number 6 was found closest to the Mètre des Archives and became the International Prototype Metre. The others were distributed to signatory states as national prototypes, and the United States received bars 21 and 27, which is how the American inch came to be legally defined in metric terms.

sections.heading: Living with an artefact: the limits of a metal bar
sections.body:
The platinum-iridium prototype was a magnificent object and an intellectual dead end, and the reasons are instructive because they apply to every artefact standard ever proposed. The first limit is reproducibility. Comparisons between the international prototype and the national copies, made with elaborate comparators at controlled temperature, could resolve differences of about 0.1 to 0.2 micrometres over a metre, which is one or two parts in ten million. That was superb for 1889 and inadequate by the 1920s, when interferometry could already do better.

The second limit is stability, and it is worse than it sounds because it is unverifiable. If every bar in the world drifts by the same amount in the same direction, no comparison between bars can detect it. The prototype was the definition, so by construction it could never be found to be wrong; any change in it was a change in the metre itself, silently propagating into every measurement ever referred to it. This is not hypothetical. The international prototype kilogram, the metre's sibling artefact, was found over a century of periodic comparisons to have diverged from the mean of its official copies by roughly 50 micrograms, about 50 parts per billion, and nobody could say which object had moved. Metrologists reasonably assumed the metre bar was subject to the same slow, invisible creep from surface contamination, hydrogen absorption and stress relaxation.

The third limit is fragility and access. There was exactly one defining metre, it lived in a vault at Sèvres under three nested bell jars, and using it meant physically transporting national bars to France. Any laboratory anywhere in the world needing length ultimately depended on that chain of custody, and on the survival of one object through two world wars fought within a few hundred kilometres of it.

The fourth limit is the sensitivity of the artefact to how it is treated. The bar's length as defined applied at 0 °C, so every practical use required a temperature correction; with a coefficient near 8.7 parts per million per kelvin, a 0.1 °C error in knowing the bar's temperature contributes 0.87 micrometres of length error, comparable to the whole comparison uncertainty. It had to sit on its Airy points, be free of vibration, and be viewed with microscopes whose own scales had to be calibrated.

Physicists had understood the escape route since the nineteenth century. In 1827 Jacques Babinet suggested that a wavelength of light would make a better standard than any bar, and James Clerk Maxwell argued in 1870 that the true natural standards of length, time and mass should be the wavelength, period and mass of molecules, because atoms of a given element are identical everywhere and do not wear out. The technology to act on that insight took another ninety years.

sections.heading: Michelson, wavelengths and the 1960 krypton definition
sections.body:
The bridge from bars to light was built by Albert Michelson. In 1892 and 1893, working at the BIPM with the French physicist René Benoît, Michelson used his interferometer to measure the international prototype metre in terms of the wavelength of the red line emitted by cadmium vapour. The answer, 1,553,163.5 wavelengths of the cadmium red line in dry air at 15 °C and standard pressure, was the first time the unit of length had been expressed in an atomic quantity, and it earned Michelson the 1907 Nobel Prize in Physics along with his other optical work.

The principle is simple to state. Light is a wave; if you split a beam, send the halves down two paths of different length, and recombine them, they interfere. When the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths the waves add and you see brightness; when it is a half-integer they cancel and you see darkness. Move one mirror steadily and the observer sees fringes sweep past, one fringe for every half wavelength of mirror travel, because the light traverses the moving arm twice. Counting fringes therefore counts half wavelengths, and if you know the wavelength you know the distance. With visible light near 600 nanometres, one fringe is about 300 nanometres, and a practised observer can estimate a fringe position to a tenth or better, giving resolution of tens of nanometres over distances of centimetres.

The catch in 1893 was that spectral lines are not infinitely sharp. Atoms in a hot gas move, and the Doppler effect spreads the emitted wavelength; they collide, which broadens it further; and if the isotopic composition is mixed, different isotopes emit at slightly different wavelengths, smearing the line. A broad line has a short coherence length, meaning fringes wash out when the two arms differ by more than a few centimetres, which limits the distance you can measure in one go.

Decades of work on lamp design solved this. The winner was krypton-86, a single isotope, in a lamp cooled to the triple point of nitrogen at 63.15 kelvin to suppress Doppler broadening, running at low current to limit collisions. Its orange-red line at about 606 nanometres, from the transition between the 2p10 and 5d5 levels, was sharp enough to give a coherence length near 80 centimetres.

In 1960 the eleventh CGPM adopted the definition: the metre is 1,650,763.73 wavelengths in vacuum of the radiation corresponding to the transition between the levels 2p10 and 5d5 of the krypton-86 atom. The odd number was chosen to make the new metre agree with the old prototype as closely as possible. For the first time the unit was reproducible in any competent laboratory from a recipe, with an uncertainty near 4 parts in 10 to the ninth, about a hundred times better than the bar. The platinum-iridium prototype was formally demoted to a historical object, though it is still preserved at Sèvres.

sections.heading: Fixing the speed of light: the 1983 definition
sections.body:
The krypton definition lasted twenty-three years and was overtaken by the laser. Stabilised lasers, particularly helium-neon lasers locked to absorption lines in iodine or methane vapour, produced light far more monochromatic than any discharge lamp — reproducible to parts in 10 to the eleventh by the late 1970s, which meant the definition itself had become the limiting error rather than the instruments.

At the same time a second thread was converging. Metrologists at the US National Bureau of Standards, led by Kenneth Evenson, measured both the frequency and the wavelength of a methane-stabilised helium-neon laser in 1972, and multiplying them gave the speed of light with an uncertainty of about 4 parts in 10 to the ninth: 299,792,456.2 metres per second, a hundredfold improvement. But that number's uncertainty was dominated entirely by the wavelength measurement, which meant by the krypton lamp. The speed of light could not be measured better than the metre was defined, and the metre could not be improved without better light.

The resolution was to cut the knot by declaration. In 1983 the seventeenth CGPM adopted the definition still in force in substance today: the metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second. The speed of light in vacuum, symbol c, became exactly 299,792,458 metres per second by definition, with zero uncertainty, forever. It is no longer a quantity to be measured; measuring it now would just be a check on your metre and your second.

Three things make this work. First, special relativity's postulate that the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all inertial observers regardless of the motion of source or observer means c is a genuine constant of nature, not a property of a particular apparatus, so anchoring a unit to it is safe. Second, the second was already defined far more accurately than the metre — since 1967 by the caesium-133 hyperfine transition at exactly 9,192,631,770 hertz, with caesium fountain clocks reaching parts in 10 to the sixteenth — so length inherits that accuracy. Third, the definition is technology-neutral: it says nothing about lasers, lamps or how you should do it, so improvements in method automatically improve the realisation without needing a new treaty.

The philosophical shift is worth naming. Before 1983 the metre was a thing and c was measured; after 1983 c is fixed and the metre is derived. The physical world did not change and no measured length shifted by an observable amount, because the numbers were chosen for continuity. What changed is which quantity carries the uncertainty. This move — fixing a constant of nature and letting the unit fall out of it — became the template for the entire 2019 reform of the SI.

sections.heading: The 2019 SI and the metre's place in the constant-based system
sections.body:
On 20 May 2019 the revised International System of Units came into force, and with it a complete change of philosophy that the metre had pioneered thirty-six years earlier. All seven base units are now defined by assigning exact numerical values to seven defining constants, with no artefacts and no material substances anywhere in the system. The kilogram is fixed by the Planck constant h at exactly 6.62607015 times 10 to the minus 34 joule seconds, which finally retired the platinum-iridium cylinder that had served since 1889. The kelvin is fixed by the Boltzmann constant, the mole by the Avogadro constant, the ampere by the elementary charge, and the candela by a luminous efficacy.

The metre's part is unchanged in substance but restated in the same grammar as the others: the metre is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum, c, to be 299,792,458 when expressed in the unit metres per second, where the second is defined in terms of the caesium frequency. Written out, one metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum in 1/299,792,458 second, exactly as before.

Two features of this architecture deserve emphasis because they are frequently misunderstood. The first is the dependency chain. Length depends on time, so the metre can never be better than the second. This is not a weakness — the second is by far the best-realised unit humanity has, currently reproducible to a few parts in 10 to the eighteenth in optical clocks, which is a thousand times finer than any length measurement in routine use. Fixing a constant transfers the hard problem to where it can best be solved.

The second is that a definition is not a method. Nothing in the wording tells a laboratory how to make a metre; it merely says what a metre is. The CIPM therefore publishes a companion document called the mise en pratique, a list of approved recipes with their achievable uncertainties, updated as technology improves without any treaty change. That separation of definition from realisation is the single most important structural idea in modern metrology, and it is why the 1983 definition has survived the invention of the frequency comb, the optical clock and everything else that has come since.

There is a subtlety worth stating honestly. Because the second itself is now under review — optical clocks based on strontium, ytterbium and aluminium ions outperform caesium by orders of magnitude, and a redefinition of the second sometime in the 2030s is widely expected — the metre's realisation will quietly improve when that happens, again without touching the metre's own words. The system is built to absorb progress.

sections.heading: The mise en pratique: three approved ways to make a metre
sections.body:
The CIPM's practical recipe document lists three methods for realising the metre, and understanding which applies where explains almost everything about how length is actually produced.

The first method is direct time of flight. Measure the time t that light takes to travel a path in vacuum and set the length to c times t. Since c is exact, the uncertainty comes entirely from the timing and from knowing the medium. This is how astronomical and geodetic distances are handled: lunar laser ranging bounces pulses off retroreflectors left by Apollo missions and Soviet Lunokhod rovers and determines the 384,400-kilometre Earth-Moon distance to a few millimetres; satellite laser ranging tracks orbiters to under a centimetre; and a builder's laser rangefinder is the same physics done cheaply. Timing resolution is the limit, and since light covers 300 millimetres per nanosecond, resolving a millimetre needs about 3.3 picoseconds of timing precision — hard, which is why short distances are not measured this way.

The second method is interferometry with a source of known frequency. Set the length to n times lambda over 2, where lambda equals c divided by the frequency f of a radiation whose frequency is known. This is the workhorse for laboratory distances from micrometres to tens of metres. You do not measure the wavelength; you measure or lock the frequency, and the exact c converts it. A helium-neon laser stabilised on the iodine-127 transition at 473.6 terahertz has a frequency reproducible to about 2 parts in 10 to the eleventh, which corresponds to 20 picometres over a metre.

The third method is to use one of the recommended radiations listed in tables the CIPM maintains, each with a stated frequency and uncertainty. These are the practical standards: the iodine-stabilised helium-neon at 633 nanometres, the methane-stabilised helium-neon at 3.39 micrometres, various stabilised diode and Nd:YAG lasers, and the optical clock transitions in strontium, ytterbium, mercury and aluminium ions which double as secondary representations of the second. A laboratory that buys a certified iodine-stabilised laser has, in effect, purchased a realisation of the metre.

The choice among the three is governed by scale. Below about a metre, interferometry dominates because fringe counting is exquisitely fine. From a metre to a few hundred metres, interferometry still works but atmospheric refractive index becomes the leading error. Beyond a kilometre, time of flight takes over because you cannot keep an interferometer's fringe count unbroken over such a path. Above about a hundred thousand kilometres, only time of flight is possible at all.

A crucial practical point runs through all three: the definition specifies vacuum. In air, light travels slower by a factor of the refractive index, about 1.000271 at 20 °C, 101.325 kilopascals and 50 percent relative humidity for red light. That 271 parts per million must be corrected for, and getting it wrong is the single largest error source in real dimensional metrology.

sections.heading: Optical frequency combs and the collapse of the frequency chain
sections.body:
Between 1983 and about 2000 the metre's definition was easy to state and appallingly difficult to realise at the highest level, because linking an optical frequency to the caesium second required a frequency chain. Caesium ticks at about 9.19 gigahertz; visible light oscillates near 470 terahertz, roughly fifty thousand times faster. Counters cannot count at optical rates, so the gap had to be bridged by a cascade of phase-locked oscillators, each multiplying the frequency of the one below using nonlinear crystals and diodes, with a klystron feeding a microwave source feeding a far-infrared laser feeding a mid-infrared laser and so on upward. Such chains filled entire laboratories, existed at only a handful of institutes worldwide, took months to set up, worked for hours at a time, and were dismantled after each measurement.

The optical frequency comb destroyed that problem, and its inventors John Hall and Theodor Hänsch shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. A mode-locked femtosecond laser emits a continuous train of extremely short pulses at a precise repetition rate f_rep, typically between 100 megahertz and 1 gigahertz. In the frequency domain that pulse train is not a single colour but a picket fence of hundreds of thousands of evenly spaced sharp lines, each at a frequency f_n equal to n times f_rep plus f_ceo, where n is an integer and f_ceo is a carrier-envelope offset arising because the wave crests slip relative to the pulse envelope. Spread through nonlinear photonic-crystal fibre, the comb can span a full optical octave.

The elegance is in how f_ceo is measured. Take a comb line at the red end of frequency f, double it in a nonlinear crystal to 2f, and beat it against the comb line already sitting near that frequency at the blue end. The beat note is exactly f_ceo, which is why the technique is called self-referencing or f-2f. Now both f_rep and f_ceo are radio frequencies that an ordinary counter can measure and a clock can discipline.

The result is a gearbox between the microwave and optical worlds with no loss of accuracy in either direction. Lock f_rep and f_ceo to a caesium or hydrogen-maser reference and every one of the comb's hundreds of thousands of teeth becomes a known optical frequency. Beat an unknown laser against the nearest tooth, measure the beat, and you have the laser's absolute frequency — hence its vacuum wavelength, hence the metre. A comb fits on a small optical table, costs a fraction of a frequency chain, and runs continuously.

Combs also enabled a direct length application: dual-comb and multi-wavelength interferometry can measure absolute distance, not merely change in distance, over tens of metres with sub-micrometre uncertainty, resolving the classic ambiguity that a single-wavelength interferometer only ever counts fringes from wherever it started.

sections.heading: Interferometry in practice: counting fringes and what spoils them
sections.body:
A displacement interferometer is the instrument that turns the abstract definition into a number on a screen, and it is worth understanding concretely because it underpins machine tools, coordinate measuring machines, lithography stages and the calibration of nearly every precision instrument.

The standard arrangement is a Michelson interferometer in heterodyne form. A stabilised laser emits two closely spaced optical frequencies with orthogonal polarisations, split typically by two or three megahertz using a Zeeman-split tube or an acousto-optic modulator. A polarising beam splitter sends one polarisation to a fixed reference retroreflector and the other to a corner-cube mounted on the moving stage. Recombined, the beams beat at the split frequency, and when the stage moves the beat shifts by the Doppler frequency. Electronics count cycles of that beat relative to a reference channel; each cycle corresponds to half a vacuum wavelength divided by the refractive index of air, and with electronic interpolation, resolutions of a nanometre or below are routine over travel of a metre or more.

Corner-cube retroreflectors are used rather than plane mirrors because they return the beam parallel to its entry regardless of tilt, so the measurement survives the small angular wobble any real stage has. Heterodyne detection is preferred over simple fringe counting because a beat frequency is immune to slow drift in laser intensity and to ambient light.

The dominant error is almost never the laser. It is the air. The refractive index of air depends on temperature at roughly minus 0.93 parts per million per kelvin, on pressure at about plus 2.7 parts per million per hectopascal, on humidity at about minus 0.01 parts per million per percent relative humidity, and on carbon dioxide concentration. Practitioners compute the correction from the Edlén equation, or its modern refinement by Birch and Downs, using measured temperature, pressure and humidity along the beam path. A one-kelvin error in air temperature over a one-metre path produces a length error near 0.93 micrometres — vastly larger than the interferometer's resolution. Laboratories therefore control air to 20.0 °C plus or minus 0.1 °C, run fans to prevent stratification, and measure conditions at several points along the beam.

Two further errors deserve naming. Dead path error occurs when part of the beam path is not common to both arms at the zero position, so the uncorrected air in that segment adds error proportional to environmental change rather than to travel. Abbe error, articulated by Ernst Abbe in 1890, arises when the measuring axis is offset from the axis of interest: an offset of 100 millimetres with a stage pitch of one arcsecond produces about 0.5 micrometres of error. Abbe's principle — that the measurement scale must lie collinear with the dimension being measured — is the most frequently violated rule in dimensional metrology.

sections.heading: Traceability: how the definition reaches an ordinary workshop
sections.body:
A definition that only a national laboratory can realise would be useless. What connects a stabilised laser at a national institute to the callipers in a machine shop is traceability, formally defined as the property of a measurement result whereby it can be related to a stated reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to the measurement uncertainty.

The chain has a characteristic shape. At the top, a national metrology institute — NIST in the United States, NPL in the United Kingdom, PTB in Germany, NRC in Canada, NMIJ in Japan — realises the metre with an iodine-stabilised laser whose frequency is checked against a comb and ultimately a caesium standard, reaching relative uncertainty of a few parts in 10 to the eleventh. That laser calibrates the institute's primary interferometer, which measures reference gauge blocks by optical interference to perhaps 30 nanometres for a 100-millimetre block. Those calibrate accredited commercial laboratories' reference blocks, typically at 50 to 100 nanometres. Those in turn calibrate a workshop's working gauge blocks at a few hundred nanometres, and the workshop uses them to set its micrometers and to verify its coordinate measuring machine, which finally measures the part at a few micrometres.

Uncertainty grows at every step, which is the price of distribution. A useful rule of thumb in industry is the test uncertainty ratio: the calibration standard should be at least four times, preferably ten times, more accurate than the tolerance being verified. Checking a part to a 20-micrometre tolerance with an instrument uncertain by 15 micrometres is not measurement, it is guessing with paperwork.

The international consistency of the top of the chain is not assumed; it is demonstrated. National institutes run key comparisons, in which the same artefact circulates and each participant measures it independently, with results published in the BIPM key comparison database. The Mutual Recognition Arrangement signed in 1999 means that a calibration certificate from an accredited laboratory in one member state is accepted in others, which is what actually allows a bearing made in Japan to fit a housing made in Germany. Accreditation to the standard ISO/IEC 17025 is the mechanism by which a commercial laboratory demonstrates competence, and it requires documented procedures, trained staff, controlled environments, and a full uncertainty budget for every calibration offered.

For a reader outside industry, the practical takeaway is that a measuring instrument's number is meaningless without three accompaniments: a calibration certificate naming what it was compared against, a stated uncertainty, and a date, because instruments drift and calibration expires. An uncalibrated digital calliper reading 12.34 millimetres asserts a precision of ten micrometres that its own mechanism, with typical accuracy of 20 to 30 micrometres and jaw wear beyond that, cannot deliver.

sections.heading: Gauge blocks, wringing and the material end of the subject
sections.body:
Gauge blocks, invented by the Swedish engineer Carl Edvard Johansson around 1896 and still called Jo blocks in workshops, are the physical embodiment of length at the working level. Each is a rectangular block of hardened steel, tungsten carbide, chrome carbide or ceramic zirconia with two opposite faces lapped flat and parallel to within a few tens of nanometres and finished to a mirror surface roughness better than 25 nanometres. The defining length is the distance from one gauging face to a flat reference plate against which the other face is wrung.

Wringing is the property that makes the system work and surprises everyone who sees it first. Slide two clean blocks together with light pressure and a slight twist, and they adhere strongly enough to hang a chain of them from one block, held by a combination of molecular attraction across a gap of a few nanometres, surface tension of the residual film of oil, and atmospheric pressure. The wrung joint adds a film thickness of roughly 10 to 25 nanometres, small enough that a stack behaves as a single block. Because of this, a set of 81 or 112 blocks can be combined to make almost any dimension in 0.001-millimetre steps up to 100 millimetres and beyond, which is why a modest box of steel can serve an entire machine shop.

Grades matter and are specified in ISO 3650 and the American standard ASME B89.1.9. Grade K blocks are calibration masters with tight flatness and parallelism but relaxed length tolerance, because their length is certified rather than assumed. Grade 0 blocks are laboratory references; grade 1 are inspection blocks; grade 2 are shop-floor working blocks. For a 25-millimetre block, tolerance runs from roughly plus or minus 0.14 micrometres at grade 0 to plus or minus 0.45 micrometres at grade 2.

Temperature is the governing practical constraint. All dimensional specifications are defined at exactly 20 °C by international agreement, a convention formalised in 1931 precisely so that parts made in different countries would agree. Steel expands at about 11.5 parts per million per kelvin, so a 100-millimetre steel gauge block warms by one kelvin and grows 1.15 micrometres, several times its grade 0 tolerance. Handling a block with bare fingers for thirty seconds transfers enough heat to matter, which is why blocks are held with gloves or tongs and left to soak on the metal reference plate for twenty minutes to an hour before use.

Care rules are simple and unforgiving: clean with a lint-free cloth and a solvent, never wring a block with a burr or a scratch, protect faces from rust with a light oil film, never leave blocks wrung together for more than a few hours or they can seize, and re-certify on a schedule set by usage.

sections.heading: Where 'length' itself becomes ambiguous
sections.body:
At high precision the question "how long is it" stops having a single clean answer, and honesty requires saying where the concept itself frays.

The first frontier is relativity. Special relativity says a measuring rod moving relative to an observer is contracted along its direction of motion by a factor of the square root of one minus v squared over c squared; length is therefore not a property of an object alone but of an object and an observer. At everyday speeds the effect is invisible — at 300 metres per second the contraction is about 5 parts in 10 to the thirteenth — but for satellite geodesy it is real and modelled. General relativity adds that spacetime is curved by mass, so the geometry itself is not Euclidean: in the vicinity of Earth, the circumference of a circle is very slightly less than 2 pi times its measured radius. Over the size of the Earth the discrepancy is a few millimetres, which is why modern reference frames such as the International Terrestrial Reference Frame are defined with an explicit relativistic model rather than as naive geometry.

The second frontier is that vacuum is not the same everywhere in a way the definition can ignore. The metre is defined for light in vacuum, but in a gravitational potential clocks run at different rates — a clock at sea level ticks slower than one a kilometre higher by about 1.1 parts in 10 to the thirteenth per kilometre — and since length is derived from time, precise length work must state its reference frame. Optical clocks are now sensitive enough to detect a height change of a centimetre through this effect, a technique called chronometric levelling.

The third frontier is that at very small scales objects do not have crisp edges. The "diameter" of an atom is a statement about an electron probability cloud, not a boundary. Measuring the width of a semiconductor line at the nanometre level requires defining which contour of a diffuse edge counts, and different techniques — atomic force microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, X-ray scattering — give systematically different answers on the same feature. The community handles this by defining measurand-specific conventions rather than pretending a unique true value exists. The X-ray crystal density method, which uses silicon lattice spacing as a natural ruler at about 543 picometres, provides a bridge from the optical world down to the atomic one.

The fourth is thermodynamic. Every object at finite temperature has atoms in constant vibration with amplitudes of picometres, so its surface is fluctuating, and a length assigned to it is a time average. Below about the picometre level, "the length of this block" is a statistical description, not a fact.

sections.heading: Failure modes and what to do when the numbers disagree
sections.body:
Most real-world length disputes are not exotic. When two competent parties measure the same feature and get different answers, the cause is nearly always one of a short list, and working through them in order resolves the great majority of cases.

Temperature is the first suspect and the most common culprit. Confirm both measurements were taken at, or corrected to, 20 °C, and that the part had actually reached that temperature rather than merely being in a controlled room. A large aluminium casting can take many hours to equilibrate, and aluminium's expansion coefficient of about 23 parts per million per kelvin is twice steel's. If the part and the instrument are made of different materials, both corrections are needed. Always record the material and the measured temperature alongside the length; a bare number without them is not a result.

The second suspect is the reference. Ask what each instrument was last calibrated against, when, and with what stated uncertainty. An out-of-calibration micrometer with a worn anvil, a coordinate measuring machine whose probe tip radius was entered wrongly, or a laser interferometer with no environmental compensation will all be confidently wrong. A quick check is to have both parties measure the same certified gauge block; if they disagree on the block, the dispute is about instruments, not the part.

The third is the definition of the measurand. Surprisingly often the two parties are measuring different things: outer diameter at different axial positions on a slightly tapered shaft, a bore that is out of round measured on different diameters, a length between surfaces that are not flat, or a feature located from a different datum. Modern geometric dimensioning and tolerancing exists to make this explicit, and its absence from a drawing is the root cause of a large fraction of inspection disagreements. Establish the datum scheme before arguing about numbers.

The fourth is measurement force and Abbe offset. A micrometer with a ratchet applies roughly 5 to 10 newtons, which elastically compresses both the part and the frame; on a thin-walled tube this can be tens of micrometres. Check that the measuring scale lies along the dimension being measured, since an offset combined with any angular error produces a proportional error.

The fifth is uncertainty itself. Two results differing by less than the combined uncertainty do not disagree at all; they agree. Compute the combined standard uncertainty by adding contributions in quadrature and expand it, conventionally by a coverage factor of two for about 95 percent confidence, following the internationally agreed Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement. A result reported without an uncertainty cannot be compared to anything, and demanding one is the single most useful habit in the whole subject.

guides.title: Writing Unit Symbols and Numbers Correctly
guides.summary: The internationally agreed rules for writing numbers, unit symbols, and prefixes — spacing, capitalization, decimal markers, compound units, and uncertainty — along with the authorities behind those rules and the costly errors they exist to prevent.

sections.heading: Why Notation Discipline Matters
sections.body: On 23 September 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter disintegrated in the Martian atmosphere at the end of a nine-month, 665-million-kilometre voyage. The navigation team at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory had been feeding its trajectory software with thruster data supplied by the spacecraft's builder, and that data expressed impulse in pound-force seconds while the software expected newton seconds. Every digit was transmitted correctly; what failed was the layer of convention that tells a reader — human or machine — what a number means. The factor of about 4.45 between the two units nudged the spacecraft roughly 170 kilometres lower than intended, below survivable altitude, and destroyed a mission that had cost about 327 million United States dollars. Unit and number notation failures rarely make headlines that large, but they injure and kill people constantly at smaller scales. In medicine, a handwritten U for units has been read as a zero, turning 10 units of insulin into 100; the symbol µg for microgram has been misread as mg, a thousandfold overdose, which is why many hospital systems ban the Greek letter entirely and require mcg on prescriptions. In 1983, Air Canada Flight 143 ran out of fuel at 12 500 metres because a fuelling calculation confused pounds with kilograms during the airline's conversion to metric; the aircraft, afterwards nicknamed the Gimli Glider, survived only through exceptional piloting. Engineering drawings, drug labels, laboratory notebooks, recipes, contracts, and customs declarations all depend on the same fragile agreement: that writer and reader share one set of rules for how quantities are written down. Those rules are not natural facts. Nothing is inevitable about writing kg rather than KG or kgs, about putting a space between 25 and °C, or about using a raised dot to multiply units. They are conventions, fixed by international agreement precisely so that a measurement written in Tokyo reads identically in Toronto and Tunis. The conventions are maintained chiefly by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures and published in the SI Brochure, with national elaborations such as the United States NIST Special Publication 811 and the ISO/IEC 80000 standards series. Because they are conventions, the only way to get them right is to learn them; intuition will happily supply plausible-looking forms — kph, sec, amps, 5kg — every one of which is wrong. The stakes justify the pedantry. A correctly written quantity carries three separable pieces of information: a numerical value, a unit that gives the number physical meaning, and, implicitly or explicitly, a statement of how precisely the value is known. Sloppy notation corrupts any of the three. Writing 2,500 m means two and a half thousand metres to an American reader and two and a half metres to much of continental Europe, where the comma is the decimal marker. Writing 3000 with no unit means nothing at all. Writing 1.0 when you actually know only 1 overstates your knowledge tenfold. The whole grammar of quantity amounts to perhaps two dozen rules, and learning them is among the cheapest insurance available against expensive, occasionally fatal, misunderstanding.

sections.heading: Who Makes the Rules: BIPM, the SI Brochure, and Friends
sections.body: The rules for writing measurements descend from a treaty. On 20 May 1875, seventeen states signed the Metre Convention in Paris, creating the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), which still operates from the Pavillon de Breteuil at Sèvres outside Paris. The Convention also created the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM), a diplomatic assembly that meets roughly every four years and holds final authority over the international measurement system, and the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM), a standing committee of eighteen scientists that prepares its decisions. In 1960 the 11th CGPM consolidated a century of piecemeal agreements into the Système international d'unités — the SI, an abbreviation kept identical in every language. The 26th CGPM in November 2018 completed the system's most profound revision, redefining the kilogram, ampere, kelvin, and mole in terms of exact fixed values of the Planck constant, the elementary charge, the Boltzmann constant, and the Avogadro constant, effective 20 May 2019; since that date no SI unit depends on any physical artefact. The canonical rulebook for writing quantities is the SI Brochure, published by the BIPM and currently in its ninth edition (2019, with subsequent updates); its fifth chapter is the closest thing in existence to an official grammar of measurement. National metrology institutes translate and elaborate it. In the United States, the National Institute of Standards and Technology publishes Special Publication 811, a practical style guide considerably more detailed than the Brochure itself, together with SP 330, the American edition of the Brochure. The international standards bodies ISO and IEC maintain the ISO/IEC 80000 series, Quantities and units, which replaced the older ISO 31 and specifies names, symbols, definitions, and typesetting rules across some thirteen parts — part 1 gives the general rules, part 3 covers space and time, part 13 covers information science and technology, and so on. Legal metrology — the law of measurement in trade — is coordinated internationally by the OIML, the International Organization of Legal Metrology, while national statutes such as the United Kingdom's Weights and Measures Act 1985 or the United States Metric Conversion Act of 1975 determine what units may lawfully appear on shop scales, fuel pumps, and packaged goods. Beneath these official layers sit publisher and discipline conventions: the ACS Style Guide in chemistry, the AMA Manual of Style in medicine, IEEE editorial standards in engineering, and the house rules of individual journals. These occasionally contradict the BIPM — the space before the percent sign is the most famous disagreement, required by the Brochure and rejected by most publishers. When authorities conflict, the working rule is straightforward: within any one document, choose the most authoritative guide your audience recognizes and apply it without exception, because consistency inside a document matters more than which defensible convention you selected. Knowing the hierarchy also tells you which rules are truly fixed — unit symbol case and prefix meanings are never negotiable — and which are merely house style, such as the percent space or the choice between a raised dot and a thin space in unit products.

sections.heading: Unit Symbols Are Symbols, Not Abbreviations
sections.body: The single most clarifying idea in the whole subject is this: kg is not an abbreviation of the word kilogram. It is a mathematical symbol, an entity of the same kind as x or π, and it obeys the grammar of mathematics rather than the grammar of prose. Almost every rule about unit symbols follows from that one fact. First, a symbol takes no full stop. You write 10 m, never 10 m., except where the symbol happens to fall at the end of a sentence and the full stop belongs to the sentence. An abbreviation such as etc. carries a period because it is a shortened word; m carries none because it is not a word at all. Second, a symbol is invariant in the plural. Five kilograms is written 5 kg, never 5 kgs; three hours is 3 h, never 3 hrs. English pluralizes nouns, but mathematics does not pluralize symbols — nobody writes that a triangle has three xs. Third, symbols are always set in upright roman type, even inside an italic passage, because italic letters are reserved by convention for quantity symbols: an italic m denotes mass, a roman m denotes the metre, and the difference is meaningful. The expression mV could be the product of a mass and a volume if both letters are italic, or one thousandth of a volt if both are roman, and careful typesetting is the only thing that separates them. Fourth, symbols are international while names are national. The word is metre in British English, meter in American English, metro in Spanish and Italian, Meter in German, and mètre in French, but the symbol is m in every one of those languages; the SI deliberately fixes the symbols so that tables, labels, and equations cross language borders untouched. Fifth, because symbols are mathematical objects they can be manipulated algebraically: kg·m/s² is a legitimate product and quotient, and dimensional analysis — cancelling and combining units exactly as one cancels variables — is a powerful check on any calculation. You cannot do algebra on the word kilogram. Sixth, symbols may not be invented, modified, or replaced by whatever contraction feels natural. The forms sec, amp, mtr, gm, and cc are folk abbreviations, not symbols; the correct forms are s, A, m, g, and cm³ (or, for the last, mL in clinical use). Finally, information about the quantity being measured must never be attached to the unit itself. Industry writes MWe for megawatts of electrical output and Nm³ for normal cubic metres of gas, but the BIPM is explicit that such qualifiers belong with the quantity, not the unit: write an electrical output of 30 MW, or a gas volume of 500 m³ at standard conditions. The unit's job is to state the scale of measurement and nothing else; the moment extra meaning is smuggled into the symbol, two readers can no longer be certain they are multiplying by the same thing, and the entire point of standardized notation is lost.

sections.heading: Capital Letters: People, Litres, and the Case-Sensitivity Trap
sections.body: Unit symbols are rigidly case-sensitive, and the capitalization rules encode real information. The base rule has two halves. A unit symbol is written in lower case — m, s, g, mol, cd, lm, lx — unless the unit is named after a person, in which case the first letter of the symbol is capitalized: N for the newton after Isaac Newton, Pa for the pascal after Blaise Pascal, J for the joule after James Prescott Joule, W for the watt after James Watt, Hz for the hertz after Heinrich Hertz, C for the coulomb, V for the volt after Alessandro Volta, Ω for the ohm after Georg Ohm, S for the siemens, T for the tesla, Wb for the weber, F for the farad after Michael Faraday, H for the henry, K for the kelvin after Lord Kelvin, A for the ampere after André-Marie Ampère, Bq for the becquerel, Gy for the gray, and Sv for the sievert. The names of those same units, however, are ordinary common nouns and stay entirely lower case in running text: a force of five newtons, a resistance of ten ohms, a dose of two grays. The name is capitalized only where any word would be — at the start of a sentence — and in the single exceptional name degree Celsius, where Celsius keeps its capital because it functions as a proper name inside the unit, giving the symbol °C. The one deliberate exception to the person rule runs the other way: the litre is not named after anyone, but because a lower-case l is nearly indistinguishable from the digit 1 in many typefaces, the 16th CGPM in 1979 sanctioned both l and L as its symbol. NIST and most American style guides require L, and it is the safer choice everywhere; the decorative script ℓ sometimes seen on packaging has never been sanctioned. The reason all this pedantry matters is that case changes meaning, sometimes by enormous factors. A lower-case k is the prefix kilo, a thousand; an upper-case K is the kelvin, a unit of temperature — there is no prefix K, and Km is strictly a kelvin-metre, not a kilometre. A lower-case m as a prefix is milli, one thousandth, while upper-case M is mega, one million: mW and MW differ by a factor of one thousand million, which in a power-plant specification is the difference between a torch bulb and a city's supply. Similarly mV and MV, mg and Mg (the megagram, better known as the tonne), s the second and S the siemens, t the tonne and T the tesla. In data storage the analogous pair is b for the bit and B for the byte, a factor of eight enshrined by IEC convention rather than the SI proper. Because these single letters do so much work, the rule of thumb is absolute: never change the case of a unit symbol for aesthetic reasons, at the start of a sentence, in a heading, or in a table — 10 KM and 10 km are different claims, and only one of them is a distance.

sections.heading: Prefixes from quecto to quetta
sections.body: The SI multiplies and divides its units through a fixed set of twenty-four prefixes, each a power of ten, and the prefix system has its own strict grammar. Ascending, the prefixes are deca (da, 10¹), hecto (h, 10²), kilo (k, 10³), mega (M, 10⁶), giga (G, 10⁹), tera (T, 10¹²), peta (P, 10¹⁵), exa (E, 10¹⁸), zetta (Z, 10²¹), yotta (Y, 10²⁴), and, since the 27th CGPM in November 2022, ronna (R, 10²⁷) and quetta (Q, 10³⁰). Descending, they are deci (d, 10⁻¹), centi (c, 10⁻²), milli (m, 10⁻³), micro (µ, 10⁻⁶), nano (n, 10⁻⁹), pico (p, 10⁻¹²), femto (f, 10⁻¹⁵), atto (a, 10⁻¹⁸), zepto (z, 10⁻²¹), yocto (y, 10⁻²⁴), ronto (r, 10⁻²⁷), and quecto (q, 10⁻³⁰). The 2022 additions were driven partly by data storage: the world's aggregate information was approaching a yottabyte, the top of the old scale. Note the case pattern: every prefix from kilo downward has a lower-case symbol, and every prefix from mega upward is upper-case, which is why Kg and KM are simply wrong — there is no upper-case kilo. A prefix attaches directly to the unit symbol with no space and no hyphen: km, µs, GHz, never k m or k-m. Only one prefix may ever be used at a time; the old millimicron (mµ) is now the nanometre (nm), and a micro-kilogram does not exist. The gram creates the system's one structural oddity: the base unit of mass is the kilogram, which already contains a prefix, so all prefixes attach to gram instead — one thousandth of a kilogram is a gram (g), one millionth is a milligram (mg), and forms such as µkg are forbidden. A subtler trap is exponentiation. When a prefixed unit is raised to a power, the exponent applies to the whole prefixed unit, prefix included: 1 cm³ means (10⁻² m)³ = 10⁻⁶ m³, not 10⁻² m³, and 1 km² is (10³ m)² = 10⁶ m², a full square kilometre, a million square metres, not a thousand. Misreading this has ruined many a land-area and dosage calculation. In practice a few prefixes dominate: engineering and science generally prefer steps of a thousand (milli, micro, kilo, mega), while hecto, deca, deci, and centi survive mainly in entrenched niches — the hectare, the hectopascal of meteorology, the centimetre, and the decilitre of clinical chemistry. Choose the prefix that puts the numerical value between about 0.1 and 1000 where practical: write 12.3 km rather than 12 300 m. Finally, computing corrupted kilo for decades by using it to mean 1024. The IEC resolved the ambiguity in 1998 with the binary prefixes kibi (Ki, 2¹⁰), mebi (Mi, 2²⁰), gibi (Gi, 2³⁰), and tebi (Ti, 2⁴⁰), now codified in IEC 80000-13: a kibibyte (KiB) is exactly 1024 bytes, and in careful writing kB means precisely 1000 bytes, however loosely the marketplace treats it.

sections.heading: The Space Between the Number and the Unit
sections.body: A quantity is the product of a number and a unit, and the space between them is not decoration — it is the multiplication sign of that product, written as whitespace. The rule is that the numerical value is always separated from the unit symbol by a space: 5 kg, 230 V, 8 h, 1.6 µm. Writing 5kg fuses a number to a symbol into a single meaningless token, and although the fused form is everywhere in casual writing, no standards body accepts it. The same rule covers temperature: the degree sign belongs to the unit, not the number, so the correct form is 25 °C — number, space, then the complete symbol °C — not 25° C and not 25°C. The kelvin, having no degree sign at all since the 13th CGPM renamed the old degree Kelvin in 1967, is simply 300 K. There are exactly three sanctioned exceptions, all of them the units of plane angle inherited from Babylonian astronomy: the degree, the arcminute, and the arcsecond close up against their number, as in a latitude of 51° 28′ 40″ or a bearing of 062°. The percent sign is the notorious battleground. The SI Brochure treats % as a unit symbol standing for the number 0.01 and therefore requires a space — 37 %, on the same footing as 37 kg — but the overwhelming majority of publishers, newspapers, and journals in English close it up as 37%, and both forms are defensible provided one is applied consistently throughout a document. Whichever spacing convention you adopt, one refinement matters more than any of them: the space between a number and its unit should be a non-breaking space, so that a line break can never strand 25 at the end of one line and °C at the start of the next. In word processors this is typically Ctrl+Shift+Space; in HTML it is the entity for a no-break space; in careful typography it is often the narrow no-break space, which sets the pair slightly tighter. The BIPM in fact recommends a thin space in professionally set text. A related rule governs what may share the space: only the numerical value and the symbol. Do not interleave words — write a mass of 5 kg, never a mass of 5 k g or 5 kilo g — and do not stack a symbol directly against a second number, as in ranges written 5-10kg, where the reader can no longer tell what the hyphen binds. When a quantity is used adjectivally in English prose with the unit spelled out, a hyphen appears instead of a space — a 35-millimetre film, a ten-kilometre run — but the hyphen never appears with the symbol form: a 35 mm film, a 10 km run. The pattern to internalize is that spacing is syntax. The space says multiply; its absence says these characters form one symbol; and every deviation from the standard placement quietly changes what the expression asserts.

sections.heading: Multiplying and Dividing Units
sections.body: Derived units are built by multiplying and dividing base units, and the notation for those operations has to be written carefully because the units themselves are multi-letter symbols that can collide. Multiplication of units is shown either by a half-high centred dot or by a thin space: torque is written N·m or N m. Simply concatenating the letters is hazardous: mN is the millinewton, while m·N is the metre-newton; ms is the millisecond, while m·s is the metre-second. The centred dot exists precisely to keep prefixes and units from being misread as one another, and the safest habit is to use it whenever two unit symbols are multiplied. The familiar kWh of electricity billing is, strictly, kW·h, though the closed-up form is so entrenched commercially that the Brochure tolerates it by custom. Division is shown in any of three equivalent ways: a solidus (m/s), a horizontal fraction bar, or a negative exponent (m·s⁻¹). The critical rule is that a solidus must never be repeated in the same expression without brackets, because m/s/s is ambiguous — it could mean m/(s/s), which is just metres, or (m/s)/s, which is acceleration. Write acceleration as m/s² or m·s⁻². Thermal conductance illustrates the same trap at higher stakes: the unit of heat transfer coefficient is W/(m²·K), and writing it W/m²·K formally means (W/m²)·K, a different quantity; only the brackets, or the fully exponent form W·m⁻²·K⁻¹, say what is meant. Chemists meet it as kJ/(mol·K) versus the sloppy kJ/mol·K. When unit names rather than symbols are written out, the words follow the same logic with the word per marking division — metre per second squared, watt per square metre kelvin — and the word per, like the solidus, should appear only once. Names and symbols must never be mixed in one expression: kilometres/hour and km per hour are both malformed; the choices are kilometres per hour or km/h. A worked example shows why the algebra of units is worth respecting. To convert 90 km/h to metres per second, replace each unit by its definition: 90 km/h = 90 × (1000 m)/(3600 s) = 25 m/s. The units cancelled and combined exactly like variables, and the same manipulation exposes errors: if a formula's units do not reduce to the unit of the quantity you claim to be computing, the formula is wrong, no matter how plausible the numbers look. This dimensional check is the single most valuable dividend the notation pays. It works only if the notation is honest — if every multiplication is marked, every division bracketed unambiguously, and no symbol quietly doing double duty as a prefix. One final prohibition: abbreviations such as ppb, cc, or mph may circulate in speech, but inside a compound expression only true SI symbols may be combined; there is no such unit as the kph, and the correct symbol km/h needs no invention.

sections.heading: Decimal Markers and Digit Grouping
sections.body: The digits of a number need two pieces of punctuation: something to mark the boundary between its integer and fractional parts, and something to group long runs of digits so a human eye can read them. Both are political minefields, and the international rules were drawn specifically to defuse them. The decimal marker may be either a point on the line or a comma; the 22nd CGPM resolved in 2003 that both are acceptable, acknowledging that English-speaking countries, China, and Japan write 3.14 while most of continental Europe and much of South America write 3,14. What is not acceptable is using the other symbol for digit grouping, because a number such as 1,234 then means one and a bit in Berlin and over a thousand in Boston. The international solution, required by the SI Brochure and ISO 80000-1, is to group digits in threes with a thin space and nothing else: 12 345.678 9 or, with the comma marker, 12 345,678 9. The space groups both directions from the marker — fractional digits are grouped in threes as well — and a four-digit integer such as 1234 may be left unspaced at the writer's discretion. Never group with apostrophes (a Swiss habit), and never let a grouping space break across a line; typographically it should be a thin or narrow no-break space. Three further rules protect the reader. A number less than one must carry a leading zero: 0.5, never .5, because a bare point is easily lost — a rule with a body count in medicine, where .5 mg read as 5 mg is a tenfold overdose, and where trailing zeros after a decimal (5.0 read as 50) are equally banned on prescriptions. A number should never be broken across a line at all if it can be helped. And a sentence should not begin with a numeral; recast the sentence or spell the number out. Machines complicate all of this. Software inherits its decimal convention from a locale setting, and a spreadsheet moved between a German and an American computer can silently reinterpret every value; comma-separated CSV files are especially treacherous in comma-decimal countries, which is why semicolon-separated files are common in Europe and why serious data exchange specifies the format explicitly (most programming languages and interchange formats such as JSON fix the point as the only decimal marker). Finance keeps its own counsel: monetary amounts conventionally retain comma grouping in English (1,234,567.89 dollars) and follow national custom elsewhere, and no international body has tried to dislodge that. The practical discipline is therefore: in scientific and technical writing use space grouping and state nothing ambiguous; in software treat the decimal marker as data about the locale, never an assumption; and when reading any foreign document, identify its convention from an unambiguous number before trusting a single value in it.

sections.heading: Significant Figures and Stating Uncertainty
sections.body: Every measured number is a claim about knowledge, and the way it is written states how much knowledge is being claimed. The informal system for this is significant figures: the digits of a number that carry information, read from the first non-zero digit. Writing a length as 1.2 m claims knowledge to roughly the nearest tenth of a metre; writing 1.20 m claims the nearest centimetre. The two are different assertions, which is why a trailing zero after a decimal point is never mere decoration and must not be added or removed casually. Ambiguity arises with integers: does 1200 m claim four significant figures or two? The plain form cannot say, and there are two honest escapes. The first is scientific notation, which makes the claim explicit — 1.2 × 10³ m claims two figures, 1.200 × 10³ m claims four. The second is choosing a prefix so the doubtful zeros disappear: 1.2 km. Converted values inherit the precision of their source, and over-precise conversion is a classic error: a hiking guide's about 10 miles should become about 16 km, not 16.093 44 km, even though the conversion factor (1 mile = 1.609 344 km exactly, and 1 inch = 25.4 mm exactly, by the 1959 international yard and pound agreement) is exact. During a multi-step calculation, keep one or two guard digits beyond what you will report and round only at the end; rounding at every intermediate step accumulates error. The default rounding rule rounds half away from zero, but computation and statistics often use round-half-to-even (2.5 rounds to 2, 3.5 rounds to 4) to avoid a systematic upward bias over many roundings — worth knowing because different software defaults differ. Formal scientific writing goes beyond significant figures and states uncertainty explicitly. The expanded form gives a value with a plus-or-minus interval, and the unit must govern both parts, so the bracketed form is required: (50.0 ± 0.3) mm, or equivalently 50.0 mm ± 0.3 mm, but not 50.0 ± 0.3 mm, which formally attaches the unit only to the uncertainty. The compact form, standard in physics and metrology, appends the uncertainty in the final digits in parentheses: the CODATA value of the electron mass is written 9.109 383 7139(28) × 10⁻³¹ kg, meaning that the last two displayed digits are uncertain by 28 — an uncertainty of 0.000 000 0028 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What the interval means (one standard deviation, a 95 percent confidence interval, an instrument's guaranteed tolerance) is not self-evident and should be stated; the international reference for the machinery is the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement, the GUM. By contrast, some numbers are exact by definition — 1000 m in a km, 12 in a dozen, the 299 792 458 m/s of the speed of light since 1983 — and take no uncertainty at all. The habit to build is simple: before writing any number, decide what you actually know, and then write exactly that many digits, no more and no fewer.

sections.heading: Ranges, Tolerances, and Dimensions
sections.body: Quantities travel in pairs and triples — ranges, tolerances, and physical dimensions — and compound expressions have their own ways of going wrong. The governing principle, stated plainly in NIST SP 811, is that a unit symbol applies only to the number it stands beside, so every number in a compound expression needs its own unit or an unambiguous bracket. A temperature range is therefore written 20 °C to 25 °C, or (20 to 25) °C, but not 20 to 25 °C and especially not 20–25 °C in precise work, because the naked 20 has no unit of its own. The en-dash range form (20–25 °C) is tolerated in tables and journalism where space is tight, but it collapses entirely when negative numbers appear — −20–−25 °C is unreadable, and −20 °C to −25 °C is not — so the word to is the robust choice everywhere. Tolerances follow the same logic: a machined length is (50 ± 0.2) mm or 50 mm ± 0.2 mm, never 50 ± 0.2 mm; a resistor is (4.7 ± 5 %) kΩ only if the bracket makes clear that the percentage applies to the value. Physical dimensions repeat the unit for each measurement: a plate is 30 mm × 50 mm, a room is 4 m × 5 m × 2.5 m, and the multiplication sign between them is the proper × (or the word by in prose), not the letter x. The form 30 × 50 mm invites a reader to wonder whether the first number is dimensionless, and in international trade documents that doubt costs money. Percentages need the same care in ranges — 5 % to 10 %, since in 5 to 10 % the 5 might be percentage points or a raw count — and interest-rate writing distinguishes further between percent and percentage points, because a rise from 10 % to 12 % is an increase of 2 percentage points but of 20 percent relative. Engineering drawings push tolerance notation furthest: a dimension may carry an asymmetric tolerance (50 +0.1/−0.3 mm), a fit class from the ISO 286 hole-and-shaft system (50 H7/g6), or a default general tolerance invoked by citing ISO 2768 in the title block, and on a drawing the unit is often declared once (all dimensions in millimetres) precisely so that repetition is unnecessary — the declaration substitutes for the per-number unit rule, and mixing units on such a drawing after the declaration is forbidden. Two smaller conventions round out the family. A ratio between like quantities can be written with a colon (a slope of 1:50), and aspect ratios follow the same pattern (16:9). And when several quantities are added or compared in a sentence, resist the temptation to let one unit govern them all silently across a conjunction: the beam carries 3 kN at one end and 5 kN at the other, with the unit stated twice, leaves nothing for a hurried reader to reconstruct.

sections.heading: Unit Names in Prose: When to Spell Things Out
sections.body: Symbols are for measurement; names are for sentences. Knowing which register you are writing in, and staying in it, is most of the craft of quantities in prose. The core pairing rule is that numerals go with symbols and spelled-out numbers go with spelled-out names: write 5 kg or five kilograms, and avoid the hybrids five kg and, in formal technical writing, 5 kilograms — though journalism and general non-fiction accept numeral-plus-name freely, and consistency within the document again outranks the choice itself. Scientific style guides generally prefer the symbol form whenever a specific measured value is stated, reserving names for quantities discussed in general: the sample gained 3.2 mg, but the effect grows by a few milligrams per cycle. A sentence may not begin with a numeral or a symbol; recast it (The mass was 5 kg) or spell everything out (Five kilograms of ore were loaded). Unit names behave as ordinary English nouns. They pluralize regularly — newtons, kelvins, henries or henrys, with hertz, lux, and siemens invariant — and they take lower case everywhere except sentence-initially and in degree Celsius. Convention on fractional values is that the plural begins beyond one: 0.5 metre and half a metre, but 1.5 metres. When a quantity is used attributively, English hyphenates the spelled form — a five-kilogram mass, a 90-minute film, a three-metre drop — but never hyphenates the symbol form: a 5 kg mass, a 90 min delay, a 35 mm lens. Compound unit names take no hyphen internally (a metre per second squared, not metre-per-second-squared) unless the whole compound is used attributively and clarity demands it. Powers of units have conventional names: square metre and cubic metre for area and volume, but second squared in acceleration — metre per second squared — because per second squared modifies the denominator. Saying units aloud follows the names, not the symbols: 5 km/h is read five kilometres per hour, and reading symbols letter by letter (five kay em per aitch) marks casual speech, harmless aloud but never to be written. Two traps deserve special notice. First, the prefix and the name fuse into one word — kilometre, microsecond, milliampere — never kilo metre or kilo-metre; and the stress in kilometre, however commonly it falls on the second syllable in speech, does not change the spelling.
