Second, informal quantity words such as kilo (for kilogram), mil (dangerously ambiguous among millilitre, millimetre, and thousandth of an inch), and click or klick (military slang for kilometre) have no place in writing that anyone might act on; mil in particular has caused real dosing and machining errors, since a US mil is 0.0254 mm while a spoken mil in a hospital usually means a millilitre. The prose register, done well, is invisible: the reader absorbs the quantity without noticing the machinery. It fails loudly when registers mix — a sentence like the car managed 40 mpg over five hundred km jars precisely because it switches system, register, and style three times in a breath.

sections.heading: Non-SI Units You May Use, and How to Write Them
sections.body: The SI coexists with a short official list of outside units accepted for use with it, and with the customary systems still lawful in several countries, and each group has fixed symbols that are just as non-negotiable as the SI's own. The accepted list, maintained in the SI Brochure, covers units too embedded in life and science to abolish. Time: the minute (min), hour (h), and day (d) — so a duration is 3 h 20 min, never 3 hrs or 3h20, and hr is not a symbol at all. Angle: the degree (°), arcminute (′), and arcsecond (″). Area: the hectare (ha), which is 10⁴ m². Volume: the litre (L or l), 10⁻³ m³. Mass: the tonne (t), 10³ kg, called the metric ton in the United States; its symbol is a lower-case t, colliding awkwardly in speech but not on paper with the imperial ton. Energy at atomic scale: the electronvolt (eV), about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Mass at atomic scale: the dalton (Da). Astronomy: the astronomical unit (au, redefined in 2012 as exactly 149 597 870 700 m). Logarithmic ratios: the neper (Np), bel (B), and in practice the decibel (dB). All of these take prefixes where sensible — mL, kt, MeV, GDa — except the time and angle units, which never do: there is no millihour. A second tier of units is tolerated in special fields but discouraged elsewhere: the bar (100 kPa exactly) and the millimetre of mercury (mmHg, about 133.3 Pa), the latter kept alive worldwide by blood-pressure measurement; the ångström (Å, 0.1 nm) in crystallography; the nautical mile (1852 m exactly) and the knot, one nautical mile per hour, in navigation and aviation. The calorie deserves its own warning: the small calorie (cal, about 4.184 J) and the large dietary Calorie (kcal) differ by a factor of a thousand and are distinguished in print sometimes only by a capital C, so careful nutritional writing uses kcal or kJ and never the bare word. The customary and imperial units still in legal use — inch, foot, yard, mile, pound, ounce, pint, gallon — have conventional symbols without full stops: in, ft, yd, mi, lb, oz, pt, gal. They form plurals like SI symbols, which is to say not at all: 5 lb, never 5 lbs, however universal lbs is on gym equipment. Because in collides with the English word in, American style sometimes permits in. with a period, or the double-prime ″ for inches and prime ′ for feet (a 6′2″ person) — an acknowledged, documented exception to the no-period rule. Remember also that the US and imperial systems diverge: a US gallon is 3.785 L while an imperial gallon is 4.546 L, and a US pint is 16 fluid ounces against the imperial 20, so any document crossing the Atlantic should state which gallon it means or, better, give the litre value in parentheses. Dual statement — 12 ft (3.7 m) — is the standard courtesy in international technical writing, with the original measurement first and the conversion rounded to matching precision.

sections.heading: Percent, Parts per Million, Angles, and Decibels
sections.body: A family of quantities is dimensionless — pure numbers, ratios of like to like — and their notation causes trouble out of proportion to their simplicity. The percent sign stands for the number 0.01, so 37 % is exactly the number 0.37; the SI treats % as a legitimate symbol (with its disputed space), but insists that it appear with a number, not embedded in prose abbreviations like %age. Two percentages can differ in two different ways, and finance and journalism are perpetually confused by them: a rate moving from 10 % to 12 % has risen by 2 percentage points and by 20 percent of its former value, and writing which one is meant is not optional. For smaller fractions, science borrowed parts-per notation: ppm for parts per million (10⁻⁶), ppb for parts per billion, ppt for parts per trillion. The BIPM accepts ppm reluctantly and warns explicitly against ppb and ppt, because billion means 10⁹ in short-scale countries and 10¹² in long-scale ones, and trillion is worse; the unambiguous alternative is either a power of ten (a mole fraction of 2 × 10⁻⁹) or an explicit unit ratio (2 nmol/mol, 5 mg/kg). Any parts-per figure is meaningless until its basis is stated — by mass, by volume, by mole — since 10 ppm of a dense contaminant by mass is a very different concentration by volume; laboratory reports write mass fraction, volume fraction, or amount fraction in full for exactly this reason. Plane angle is formally dimensionless too (arc length over radius), and its SI unit, the radian (rad), can be treated as the number one, which is why angular frequency in rad/s and ordinary frequency in Hz are numerically different statements about the same rotation — a point that has wrecked more than one vibration calculation: 50 Hz is 314.16 rad/s. The degree and its sexagesimal subdivisions remain accepted, and decimal degrees (51.4778°) are preferred to minutes and seconds in modern data. Logarithmic quantities carry their own symbol discipline. The bel expresses a power ratio as its base-ten logarithm, and the practical decibel is one tenth of that: a power ratio of 100 is 20 dB, and because power goes as the square of amplitude, a field or voltage ratio of 100 is 40 dB. A decibel figure is meaningless without its reference, which is welded onto the symbol in forms the SI frowns at but the world uses: dBm (referred to one milliwatt), dBW, dB SPL (sound pressure referred to 20 µPa, the nominal threshold of human hearing), dBi (antenna gain against an isotropic radiator). Careful writing states the reference in words at first use. The neper (Np), based on natural logarithms, survives in transmission-line theory; 1 Np is about 8.686 dB. Finally pH, the negative decimal logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity, is written with a lower-case p and upper-case H, takes no unit, and — like all logarithmic measures — cannot be averaged or added as if it were linear: mixing equal volumes of pH 4 and pH 6 water does not give pH 5.

sections.heading: A Catalogue of Common Errors
sections.body: Most unit-writing errors fall into a dozen recurring families, and recognizing them by sight is faster than re-deriving the rules each time. The invented symbol: kph for km/h, mps for m/s, sec for s, amp for A, mtr for m, gm for g, hrs for h, mins for min. None of these exists in any standard; several (sec, amp) are acceptable spoken shorthand that must still never be written in technical text. The pluralized symbol: kgs, cms, lbs, kms. Symbols never take an s, and the reader of Kms cannot even tell whether kelvins, kilometres, or thousands were meant. The case error: KM, Kg, KHz (the prefix k is lower case); mhz for MHz; w for W. Since case selects among different prefixes and units, these are not typographical blemishes but changed meanings. The obsolete unit: degree Kelvin (°K) was abolished in 1967 — it is simply the kelvin, K; the micron was formally replaced by the micrometre (µm) in the same era, though the word survives in engineering speech; the cycle per second became the hertz in 1960. The ambiguous relic: cc for the cubic centimetre persists in medicine and motoring, but clinical safety bodies, including the Institute for Safe Medication Practices, list cc among error-prone abbreviations because handwritten it resembles 00, and require mL instead; the same do-not-use lists ban U for units (write units), IU (write international units), QD and QOD for daily dosing, the trailing zero (5.0 mg), and the naked decimal (.5 mg) — each entry paid for in patient harm. The false attachment: Nm³ for normal cubic metre, MWe for electrical megawatt, %wt for mass percent; qualify the quantity in words instead. The register error: K for thousand in financial shorthand (a $50K salary) collides with the kelvin and belongs, at most, in informal prose; the same goes for MM for million in banking, which in SI logic reads as millimillion — nothing at all. The mixed-system muddle: quoting fuel economy in mpg against consumption in L/100 km without conversion (they are reciprocal, so their scales run opposite ways — a bigger mpg is better, a bigger L/100 km worse), or mixing US and imperial gallons silently, or converting a temperature difference as though it were a temperature (a change of 10 °C is a change of 18 °F, not 50 °F, because the offset of 32 applies only to absolute temperatures, not to differences). The weight-mass conflation: the kilogram measures mass; the newton measures force; bathroom scales calibrated in kg are, strictly, inferring mass from force in standard gravity of 9.806 65 m/s², and engineering documents that write kg where they mean kgf (kilogram-force, an obsolete unit equal to 9.806 65 N) have caused structural miscalculations. Finally the billion problem: outside unit symbols entirely, the words billion and trillion still differ across languages and eras, so international documents give 10⁹ or the full digits. Reading through this rogues' gallery once a year is cheap; every entry in it was learned somewhere at real expense.

sections.heading: Typography, Keyboards, and Checking Your Work
sections.body: Correct notation finally has to be produced on real keyboards and survive real software, and a handful of character-level choices separate professional from broken output. The micro prefix is the traditional micro sign µ (Unicode U+00B5) or the Greek small mu μ (U+03BC); Unicode now recommends the Greek letter for new text, both render identically in most fonts, and the one unforgivable substitute is the Latin u — 10 ug is not a mass. The degree sign is U+00B0, not a superscript letter o or the masculine ordinal º. Angle minutes and seconds are the prime ′ (U+2032) and double prime ″ (U+2033), not apostrophes and quotation marks, which smart-quote features will silently curl into errors. The minus sign is U+2212, matching the plus sign's width; the hyphen-minus on the keyboard is tolerable in plain text but wrong in typeset work, and a negative exponent set with a hyphen (m·s⁻¹ versus m·s-1) is the visible difference. Multiplication in dimensions uses × (U+00D7), never the letter x; the unit product dot is U+22C5 or the middle dot U+00B7. Superscripts two and three exist as single characters (², ³, U+00B2 and U+00B3), and full superscript styling handles the rest. The spaces of quantity writing are the no-break space U+00A0, the thin space U+2009, and the narrow no-break space U+202F — the last being the ideal separator both between number and unit and inside digit grouping, because it can never break at a line end. Where none of this is available — source code, plain-text email, legacy instrumentation — declare an ASCII fallback and use it consistently: m^2 or m2 for the square metre, um or, better, the spelled-out micro- for µ, ohm written as the word, 1e-6 notation for powers of ten. Well-known interchange conventions exist for exactly this purpose, and the UCUM (Unified Code for Units of Measure) standard used in healthcare messaging defines case-sensitive ASCII codes for every unit so that machines need never guess. Software adds its own hazards: spreadsheets strip trailing zeros and reinterpret entries (the gene-naming community was famously forced to rename genes like SEPT2 because Excel read them as dates — measurement data deserves the same paranoia), autocorrect changes straight primes to quotes, and PDF extraction turns thin spaces into nothing, fusing numbers to units. Defend against all of it with a final audit pass: read the document once looking only at quantities. Check that every number has its unit, every unit its space, every symbol its correct case; recompute one converted value at random; run a dimensional check on any formula; confirm the decimal convention is declared or obvious; and confirm that significant figures match what was actually measured. When an error is found after release, correct it at the source and propagate the correction — an erratum, a revised drawing, a recalled label — rather than annotating downstream copies, because measurement errors metastasize through every document that cites them. The rules in the end are few, mechanical, and learnable in an afternoon; what they buy, applied every time without exception, is the quiet certainty that the number the reader receives is the number you meant.

guides.title: The SI Base Units and Their Definitions
guides.summary: A complete reference on the International System of Units: the seven defining constants and the seven base units they now fix, the physics behind each definition, how the units are realised and disseminated, the prefixes and writing conventions, and the ways unit errors cause real failures.

sections.heading: Why a system of units matters
sections.body:
A measurement is a comparison. When you say a plank is two metres long, you are saying it is twice as long as an agreed reference. The number alone is meaningless: two of what? Every quantitative statement in science, engineering, trade and medicine therefore depends on a shared, stable, reproducible answer to that question, and the machinery that supplies it is a system of units. The International System of Units, universally abbreviated SI from the French Système international d'unités, is that machinery for essentially the whole world.

Before such systems existed, units were local and physical. A foot was somebody's foot. The English yard was reputedly the distance from Henry I's nose to his thumb. Grain weights derived from actual barley grains. This worked within a village and failed catastrophically between them. Eighteenth-century France alone is estimated to have used something like a quarter of a million distinct local units of weight and measure, many with the same name but different magnitudes in neighbouring towns, which made fraud easy and honest long-distance trade hard. The problem was not merely inconvenience; it was that no two people could reliably check each other's work.

A good unit system solves several problems at once. It supplies a common language so a component machined in one country fits an assembly in another. It supplies stability over time, so a measurement made in 1950 can be compared with one made today. It supplies a chain of comparison, called traceability, so that a scale in a shop can be shown by an unbroken sequence of calibrations to agree with the international definition. And it supplies coherence, meaning the units combine through the equations of physics without stray conversion factors, so that force in newtons equals mass in kilograms times acceleration in metres per second squared, with no fudge number.

The practical stakes are enormous and mostly invisible. Global trade in goods measured by weight, volume or energy content runs to tens of trillions of currency units annually, and every transaction assumes both parties mean the same thing by a kilogram. Semiconductor manufacture places features a few nanometres wide and depends on length metrology at the picometre level. Radiotherapy delivers doses where a ten percent error in absorbed dose can mean the difference between cure and either recurrence or serious injury. Satellite navigation works only because clocks agree to nanoseconds, which corresponds to about thirty centimetres of position error per nanosecond of timing error.

The SI is maintained by an international treaty organisation and revised deliberately and rarely. Its most recent and most philosophically significant revision, effective 20 May 2019, completed a two-century project by severing every unit from any physical object and anchoring the whole system to constants of nature instead. Understanding what that means, and what each of the seven base units now actually is, is the subject of what follows.

sections.heading: From artefacts to constants: a two-century history
sections.body:
The metric system was born of the French Revolution. In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences proposed a metre defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along the meridian through Paris, and a gram as the mass of a cubic centimetre of water at the temperature of melting ice. Both definitions had a deliberate political character: they were meant to be drawn from nature and therefore to belong to everyone, in the slogan of the time, for all people, for all time. Delambre and Méchain spent seven arduous years, from 1792 to 1799, surveying the meridian arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona through a country at war to fix the length.

The practical outcome, however, was a pair of physical objects. In 1799 platinum standards, the mètre des Archives and the kilogramme des Archives, were deposited in Paris, and from that moment the definitions were effectively those bars and cylinders rather than the Earth or the water. The survey itself contained a small error, partly from an unresolved mistake Méchain concealed, so the metre is roughly 0.2 millimetres short of its intended one ten-millionth of the quadrant, a discrepancy that no longer matters because the artefact, not the Earth, became the standard.

International adoption followed. The Metre Convention was signed in Paris on 20 May 1875 by seventeen states, creating the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, known by its French initials BIPM, at Sèvres near Paris, along with the General Conference on Weights and Measures, the CGPM, which meets every four years and holds ultimate authority. In 1889 the first CGPM sanctioned the International Prototype of the Metre and the International Prototype of the Kilogram, both made of a platinum-iridium alloy chosen for hardness and chemical stability, with copies distributed to member states.

The twentieth century steadily replaced artefacts with physical phenomena. In 1960 the eleventh CGPM formally adopted the name Système International d'Unités and redefined the metre in terms of a wavelength of krypton-86 radiation. In 1967 the second was redefined atomically in terms of caesium. In 1983 the metre was redefined again by fixing the speed of light, an elegant move that turned a measurement into a definition. By the 1990s only the kilogram remained an object.

That object was a problem. Periodic comparisons of the international prototype with its official copies showed relative divergence of roughly fifty micrograms over a century, and because the prototype defined the kilogram by fiat, it could not itself be wrong; everything else in the world had to be considered to have changed. The remedy, agreed at the twenty-sixth CGPM in November 2018 and effective 20 May 2019, was to fix the numerical values of seven defining constants and derive every unit from them, retiring the last artefact after 130 years of service.

sections.heading: The architecture of the SI: constants, base units, derived units
sections.body:
The modern SI is best understood as a three-layer structure, and the top layer is the one most people have never heard of. Since 2019 the system is defined not by seven units but by seven defining constants whose numerical values, expressed in SI units, are fixed exactly by decree and can never again be measured, only used.

Those constants are the caesium hyperfine transition frequency, written with the symbol for delta nu caesium, fixed at 9 192 631 770 hertz; the speed of light in vacuum, c, fixed at 299 792 458 metres per second; the Planck constant, h, fixed at 6.626 070 15 times ten to the minus thirty-four joule seconds; the elementary charge, e, fixed at 1.602 176 634 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs; the Boltzmann constant, k, fixed at 1.380 649 times ten to the minus twenty-three joules per kelvin; the Avogadro constant, fixed at 6.022 140 76 times ten to the twenty-three per mole; and the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 terahertz, fixed at 683 lumens per watt.

From these follow the seven base units: the second for time, symbol s; the metre for length, m; the kilogram for mass, kg; the ampere for electric current, A; the kelvin for thermodynamic temperature, K; the mole for amount of substance, mol; and the candela for luminous intensity, cd. It is important to grasp that base is now an organisational convenience rather than a claim of logical priority. In the old system each base unit had its own independent definition and derived units were built from them. In the new system the constants come first and the base units are simply seven convenient quantities expressed in terms of those constants, several of which depend on more than one constant at once.

The third layer is derived units, formed as products of powers of base units. Some have special names: the newton is a kilogram metre per second squared, the joule is a newton metre, the watt is a joule per second, the pascal is a newton per square metre. Twenty-two derived units carry special names and symbols, and any other combination is expressed directly, as with metres per second or kilograms per cubic metre.

The property tying this together is coherence. A coherent system has no numerical factors other than one in the relations between units. Because the newton is defined so that one newton accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared, Newton's second law is written with no constant. This is why the SI is used in physics and the older systems with pounds-force, slugs and gravitational constants are not: coherence eliminates a whole class of arithmetic error. The dependency chain also matters practically, since the second underlies almost everything else and is by far the most accurately realised unit.

sections.heading: The second: caesium, hyperfine structure and atomic time
sections.body:
The second is the foundation of the whole system, the most accurately realised unit humanity possesses, and the one on which the metre, the ampere, the kilogram and the candela all ultimately depend. Its definition reads that the second is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the caesium frequency, the unperturbed ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom, to be 9 192 631 770 when expressed in the unit hertz, which is equal to inverse seconds.

The physics behind that number is worth unpacking. A caesium-133 atom has a single outer electron, and both that electron and the nucleus possess magnetic moments. The interaction between them, called hyperfine coupling, splits the ground state into two levels of very slightly different energy, separated by about 3.8 microelectronvolts. An atom can be driven between these two levels by microwave radiation of exactly the right frequency, and that resonance is astonishingly sharp and, so far as physics can tell, identical for every caesium-133 atom anywhere in the universe and at any time. Counting 9 192 631 770 cycles of that radiation defines one second.

The word unperturbed carries a great deal of weight. Real atoms sit in stray magnetic fields, experience thermal radiation, collide with each other and move, and all of these shift the resonance slightly. A primary caesium standard must measure each perturbation and correct for it, and the resulting uncertainty budget, listing effects such as the second-order Zeeman shift, the blackbody radiation shift and the relativistic time dilation from atomic motion, is the real intellectual content of the instrument.

The first caesium beam clock was built by Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the National Physical Laboratory in 1955, and the atomic definition was adopted in 1967 at the thirteenth CGPM, replacing a definition based on the Earth's orbit. Modern caesium fountain clocks launch a cloud of laser-cooled atoms upward through a microwave cavity and let them fall back through it, giving an interaction time of about a second and a fractional uncertainty around one part in ten to the sixteenth, roughly one second in three hundred million years.

Optical clocks, which use transitions at hundreds of terahertz rather than nine gigahertz in ions such as aluminium and ytterbium or in neutral strontium lattices, are now some hundred times better still, reaching parts in ten to the eighteenth. Because the SI second is defined by caesium, these clocks cannot be more accurate than the definition allows even though the instruments are; a redefinition of the second in terms of an optical transition is under active consideration and is widely expected in the 2030s. International Atomic Time is generated by combining several hundred clocks worldwide, and Coordinated Universal Time is that scale offset by leap seconds to track the Earth's irregular rotation, a practice the CGPM voted in 2022 to end by 2035.

sections.heading: The metre: fixing the speed of light
sections.body:
The metre is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum to be 299 792 458 when expressed in metres per second, where the second is defined by the caesium frequency. In everyday language, one metre is the distance travelled by light in vacuum in 1/299 792 458 of a second.

This definition, adopted in 1983 at the seventeenth CGPM, embodies a conceptual move that recurs throughout the modern SI and is worth pausing on because it strikes many people as circular or arbitrary. Before 1983, the speed of light was a quantity to be measured, and experimenters worked to determine it ever more precisely in terms of independently defined metres and seconds. By the early 1980s those measurements had become so good that the dominant uncertainty was in the realisation of the metre itself, not in the light. In other words, people were no longer measuring the speed of light; they were using light to measure the metre badly. The rational response was to stop measuring and start defining: declare the speed of light to be exactly that number and let the metre follow. The value chosen was the best measured value at the time, so no practical discontinuity occurred.

A consequence often misunderstood is that the speed of light in vacuum now has zero uncertainty by construction. It is not that we have measured it perfectly; it is that it is no longer a measured quantity at all. Any future experiment that appeared to find a different value would be interpreted as a change in the realisation of the metre.

Realising the metre in practice is done in three ways. The most direct is time of flight: measure how long light takes to travel a distance. This dominates at large scales, in satellite laser ranging, in lunar laser ranging to the retroreflectors left by Apollo missions, and in satellite navigation, where the position solution is essentially a set of light-travel-time measurements. At laboratory scales, time of flight is impractical because light crosses a metre in 3.3 nanoseconds, so interferometry is used instead: a stabilised laser of accurately known frequency produces a wavelength, computed as the speed of light divided by the frequency, and a displacement is measured by counting interference fringes, each corresponding to half a wavelength, typically around 316 nanometres for a helium-neon laser at 633 nanometres.

The third route uses recommended radiations, a published list of atomic and molecular transitions with agreed frequencies, most notably iodine-stabilised helium-neon lasers, which allow a national laboratory to realise the metre to a few parts in ten to the eleventh without owning a frequency comb. Optical frequency combs, developed around 2000 and recognised by the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physics, now link optical frequencies directly to the caesium second and have made length and frequency metrology a single discipline.

sections.heading: The kilogram: the Planck constant and the Kibble balance
sections.body:
The kilogram is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Planck constant to be 6.626 070 15 times ten to the minus thirty-four when expressed in the unit joule second, which is equal to kilogram metre squared per second. Since the metre and the second are themselves fixed by the speed of light and the caesium frequency, this equation can be rearranged to yield the kilogram.

That this works at all can seem baffling, because the Planck constant governs quantum mechanics and appears to have nothing to do with a lump of metal. The link is dimensional. A joule second has dimensions of mass times length squared over time. If you fix the numerical value of a quantity with those dimensions, and you have already fixed length and time, mass is thereby determined. The constant is a fact about the universe rather than a property of an object, so the definition cannot drift, be scratched or absorb contamination, all genuine concerns about the platinum-iridium cylinder it replaced.

Two experimental methods realise the kilogram. The X-ray crystal density method builds a near-perfect sphere of isotopically enriched silicon-28, measures its diameter and its lattice spacing by X-ray interferometry, and counts the atoms by arithmetic. The spheres are among the roundest objects ever made; scaled to the size of the Earth, the deviation from roundness would be a few metres.

The more widely used method is the Kibble balance, invented by Bryan Kibble at the National Physical Laboratory in 1975 and originally called the watt balance. It compares mechanical power with electrical power, and its beauty is that it never requires knowing the geometry of its own coil.
steps: Weighing mode: suspend the test mass from a coil sitting in a strong radial magnetic field, and pass a current through the coil so the upward magnetic force exactly balances the weight. The balance condition is that mass times local gravity equals current times the product of magnetic flux density and coil wire length.

Measure the current using a resistor calibrated against the quantum Hall effect and a voltage measured against a Josephson junction array, tying the electrical quantities to the Planck constant and the elementary charge rather than to artefact standards.

Measure the local gravitational acceleration at the exact position of the mass with an absolute gravimeter, typically a free-falling corner cube tracked interferometrically. Gravity varies enough across a single laboratory bench to matter.

Moving mode: switch off the current and instead move the same coil vertically through the same field at a measured, steady velocity, recording the voltage induced across it. That voltage equals velocity times the same flux-density and wire-length product.

Divide one relation by the other. The magnetic flux density and coil length appear in both and cancel exactly, which is why the field never has to be characterised. What remains equates mechanical power with electrical power.

Express that electrical power in quantum terms. The Josephson and quantum Hall effects give voltage and resistance in combinations of the Planck constant and the elementary charge, so the result yields the mass directly from the fixed value of the Planck constant.

sections.heading: The ampere: counting elementary charges
sections.body:
The ampere is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the elementary charge to be 1.602 176 634 times ten to the minus nineteen when expressed in coulombs, where the coulomb is an ampere second. Rearranged, one ampere is the electric current corresponding to the flow of 1/(1.602 176 634 times ten to the minus nineteen) elementary charges per second, which works out to approximately 6.241 509 times ten to the eighteen electrons past a point each second.

This is a much more intuitive definition than the one it replaced, and the contrast is instructive. From 1948 to 2019 the ampere was defined as the constant current which, maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible circular cross-section placed one metre apart in vacuum, would produce a force between them of two times ten to the minus seven newtons per metre of length. Every word of that definition describes something impossible. No conductor is infinitely long or of negligible cross-section, and no laboratory contains a perfect vacuum with nothing else in it. The definition therefore had to be approximated by current balances with elaborate corrections, and it fixed the magnetic constant, the permeability of free space, at exactly four pi times ten to the minus seven henries per metre. After the 2019 revision that constant became an experimentally determined quantity again, though still known to about one part in ten to the tenth, since it is tied to the fine-structure constant.

Practical realisation of electrical units barely uses the formal definition at all, because two quantum effects provide far better standards. The Josephson effect, predicted by Brian Josephson in 1962 and worth the 1973 Nobel Prize, causes a superconducting junction irradiated with microwaves of frequency f to develop precisely quantised voltage steps of magnitude n times h f divided by 2e. Since h and e are now exact and frequency is measured against the caesium second, this yields an exact voltage. Arrays of tens of thousands of junctions produce convenient volts rather than microvolts.

The quantum Hall effect, discovered by Klaus von Klitzing in 1980 and recognised with the 1985 Nobel Prize, causes a two-dimensional electron gas in a strong magnetic field at low temperature to exhibit Hall resistance plateaux at exactly the von Klitzing constant, h divided by e squared, approximately 25 812.807 ohms, divided by an integer. This too is now exact.

With exact voltage and exact resistance, Ohm's law gives exact current, and modern metrology realises the ampere this way to parts in ten to the ninth or better. Single-electron pumps, which shuttle charges one at a time at a clock frequency, realise the definition literally but at currents of only picoamperes; closing the quantum metrology triangle by checking that all three routes agree remains an active research programme.

sections.heading: The kelvin: the Boltzmann constant and thermodynamic temperature
sections.body:
The kelvin is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Boltzmann constant to be 1.380 649 times ten to the minus twenty-three when expressed in joules per kelvin, where the joule is a kilogram metre squared per second squared. The Boltzmann constant is the conversion factor between temperature and energy per degree of freedom: a particle in thermal equilibrium at temperature T carries on average one half of k times T of kinetic energy per translational degree of freedom. Fixing k therefore states, in effect, that one kelvin is the temperature change corresponding to a thermal energy change of 1.380 649 times ten to the minus twenty-three joules.

The previous definition, in force from 1954 to 2019, set the triple point of water at exactly 273.16 kelvin. The triple point is the unique combination of temperature and pressure, about 611.66 pascals, at which ice, liquid water and water vapour coexist in equilibrium, and it is reproducible in a sealed glass cell to a few tens of microkelvin. Its weakness was that the reproducibility depended on the water. Isotopic composition matters, since heavy water raises the triple point measurably, which forced a further specification of Vienna Standard Mean Ocean Water, and dissolved impurities depress it. Moreover the definition anchored the scale at one point only, so accuracy degraded badly far from 273 kelvin, which is precisely where much interesting physics happens.

Because the kelvin is now defined through energy, it can be realised at any temperature by measuring energy directly, and several primary thermometers do exactly that. Acoustic gas thermometry measures the speed of sound in a dilute monatomic gas such as argon in a precision spherical resonator; the speed of sound squared is proportional to k T divided by the particle mass, and extrapolating to zero pressure removes non-ideality. This method delivered the most accurate determinations of k before the redefinition, at about one part in a million. Dielectric constant gas thermometry measures how a gas changes the capacitance of a capacitor, exploiting helium's calculable polarisability. Johnson noise thermometry measures the tiny random voltage fluctuations across a resistor, whose mean square is proportional to k T times resistance times bandwidth, and is valuable at high temperatures. Radiometric thermometry uses Planck's radiation law directly and dominates above about 1300 kelvin.

In everyday practice almost no one uses a primary thermometer. Instead the International Temperature Scale of 1990, known as ITS-90, provides a practical recipe: a set of seventeen defined fixed points, such as the triple point of hydrogen at 13.8033 kelvin and the freezing point of copper at 1357.77 kelvin, with specified interpolating instruments between them, chiefly platinum resistance thermometers. The degree Celsius is defined as exactly one kelvin in size, with zero degrees Celsius equal to 273.15 kelvin, so a temperature difference is numerically identical in either unit.

sections.heading: The mole: amount of substance and the Avogadro constant
sections.body:
The mole is defined as containing exactly 6.022 140 76 times ten to the twenty-three elementary entities, this number being the fixed numerical value of the Avogadro constant when expressed in the unit per mole. The definition adds an essential qualification: an elementary entity may be an atom, a molecule, an ion, an electron, any other particle or a specified group of particles, and the entity must always be stated. A mole of oxygen is ambiguous and therefore meaningless; a mole of oxygen atoms and a mole of oxygen molecules differ by a factor of two in mass.

The mole is unusual and mildly controversial among the base units because amount of substance is arguably not a dimension of nature at all but a count, and counts are dimensionless. Some metrologists have argued the mole is really a unit like the dozen. The counterargument, which prevailed, is that chemistry needs a unit that connects the macroscopic world of grams and litres to the microscopic world of particles, and that treating amount of substance as its own quantity prevents a great deal of confusion. In practice the mole is what makes stoichiometry work: a balanced chemical equation is a statement about numbers of particles, and the mole converts that into masses you can weigh.

The 2019 definition changed something subtle but important. Previously the mole was defined as the amount of substance containing as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 0.012 kilograms of carbon-12, which locked the mole to the kilogram and made the molar mass of carbon-12 exactly twelve grams per mole by definition. Now the mole is defined purely as a count and is entirely independent of the kilogram. As a consequence the molar mass of carbon-12 is no longer exact; it is an experimentally determined quantity equal to 11.999 999 9958 grams per mole with a relative uncertainty of about three parts in ten to the tenth. For any practical chemistry, twelve grams per mole remains correct to far more figures than anyone needs, but the change matters for high-precision mass spectrometry.

The molar mass constant, formerly exactly one gram per mole, is likewise now measured. The unified atomic mass unit, or dalton, is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a free carbon-12 atom at rest in its ground state, approximately 1.660 539 times ten to the minus twenty-seven kilograms, and remains the practical unit of atomic and molecular mass.

Realisation in the laboratory is largely by weighing a pure substance of known molar mass, so accuracy depends on purity assay and on isotopic composition, both of which are frequently the dominant uncertainty in analytical chemistry. The silicon-28 sphere experiment is the one true primary realisation, counting atoms in a crystal by measuring volume and lattice spacing.

sections.heading: The candela: the one unit built around human biology
sections.body:
The candela is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the luminous efficacy of monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 times ten to the twelve hertz to be 683 when expressed in lumens per watt. Unpacked: a source emitting monochromatic green light at 540 terahertz, corresponding to a wavelength of about 555 nanometres in air, with a radiant intensity of 1/683 watts per steradian in a given direction, has a luminous intensity of one candela in that direction.

The candela is the odd one out, and it is worth being explicit about why. The other six base units concern physical quantities that exist independently of observers. The candela does not. It measures light as weighted by the response of the human visual system, and it exists because engineering lighting for people requires a quantity that tracks perceived brightness rather than raw power. A watt of deep red light at 700 nanometres and a watt of green light at 555 nanometres carry identical energy but differ in apparent brightness by a factor of roughly two hundred, because the retina is far more sensitive to green. Any unit useful for lighting design must encode that.

The encoding is a standard curve. The photopic luminous efficiency function, written V of lambda, was adopted by the International Commission on Illumination in 1924 from experiments on a modest number of observers, and it peaks at 555 nanometres, which is why that wavelength was chosen for the definition, and falls to essentially zero below about 380 and above about 780 nanometres. The value 683 was chosen for continuity with the earlier definition based on the light emitted by a black body at the freezing point of platinum, 2045 kelvin, so that existing lighting measurements did not shift. A separate scotopic curve, peaking at 507 nanometres, describes dark-adapted rod vision, and the intermediate mesopic range remains an area of genuine practical disagreement in road-lighting standards.

The candela anchors a family of photometric units. Luminous flux, the total light output of a source, is measured in lumens, a lumen being a candela steradian; a typical domestic LED bulb emits 800 to 1500 lumens. Illuminance, the light falling on a surface, is measured in lux, one lux being one lumen per square metre; office lighting standards specify 300 to 500 lux on a desk, an overcast day gives around 1000 lux and direct sunlight around 100 000 lux. Luminance, the brightness of a surface as seen, is measured in candelas per square metre, with typical computer displays at 250 to 400 and high-dynamic-range displays reaching 1000 or more.

Realisation is by absolute radiometry: a cryogenic electrical substitution radiometer measures optical power by comparing the heating it produces with electrical heating, achieving uncertainties near one part in ten thousand, after which the V of lambda weighting converts radiometric to photometric quantities. The residual uncertainty in practical photometry is dominated not by the radiometry but by how well a detector's spectral response matches the standard curve.

sections.heading: Derived units and the principle of coherence
sections.body:
Only seven quantities are base; everything else is derived by multiplying and dividing them. Speed is metres per second, acceleration metres per second squared, density kilograms per cubic metre, and so on without limit. Twenty-two of these combinations occur so often that they have been given special names and symbols, and knowing them is most of practical numeracy in science and engineering.

The mechanical group runs as follows. The hertz is one per second, for periodic phenomena. The newton is a kilogram metre per second squared, the force that accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared; a medium apple weighs about one newton on Earth. The pascal is a newton per square metre, a very small pressure, since standard atmospheric pressure is 101 325 pascals. The joule is a newton metre, the work done pushing with one newton through one metre; a joule is roughly the energy to lift that apple one metre. The watt is a joule per second. The radian and steradian, for plane and solid angle, are dimensionless ratios treated as derived units.

The electromagnetic group comprises the coulomb, an ampere second; the volt, a watt per ampere; the farad, a coulomb per volt; the ohm, a volt per ampere; the siemens, the reciprocal ohm; the weber for magnetic flux; the tesla, a weber per square metre; and the henry for inductance. The remaining special names cover the degree Celsius; the lumen and lux for light; the becquerel, one nuclear decay per second, and the gray, a joule per kilogram of absorbed radiation dose, and the sievert, the same physical dimensions but weighted for biological effect; and the katal, one mole per second of catalytic activity.

Coherence is the property that binds these together, and it is the SI's most underappreciated virtue. A system is coherent when every derived unit is a product of powers of base units with a numerical factor of exactly one. The practical payoff is that if you insert quantities in coherent SI units into any correct physical equation, the answer emerges in coherent SI units with no conversion factor to remember or forget. Pressure equals force over area: put newtons and square metres in, get pascals out. Power equals voltage times current: put volts and amperes in, get watts out. Kinetic energy is half the mass times velocity squared: kilograms and metres per second in, joules out.

Contrast this with customary systems, where computing pressure in pounds per square inch from pounds of force requires care about whether the pound is mass or force, and where the gravitational conversion constant appears in engineering formulae as a permanent trap. Note one important subtlety: coherence holds for base units, not for prefixed ones. Substituting grams for kilograms, or centimetres for metres, breaks the property and reintroduces factors, which is a frequent source of error in student calculations.

sections.heading: Prefixes: from quecto to quetta
sections.body:
The decimal prefixes are the feature most people meet first and the reason the SI is easy to use across scales spanning sixty orders of magnitude. A prefix multiplies the unit by a power of ten, and prefix plus unit symbol forms a single new symbol with no space and no hyphen: a kilometre is km, a millisecond ms, a microgram, using the Greek letter mu, a symbol frequently written as ug when the character is unavailable.

The multiplying prefixes are deca for ten, hecto for a hundred, kilo for a thousand, mega for ten to the six, giga for ten to the nine, tera for ten to the twelve, peta for ten to the fifteen, exa for ten to the eighteen, zetta for ten to the twenty-one, yotta for ten to the twenty-four, and, added at the twenty-seventh CGPM in November 2022, ronna for ten to the twenty-seven and quetta for ten to the thirty. The dividing prefixes are deci, centi, milli, micro, nano, pico, femto, atto, zepto, yocto and, from the same 2022 decision, ronto for ten to the minus twenty-seven and quecto for ten to the minus thirty. The 2022 additions were driven partly by data storage, which was approaching yottabytes and had no headroom, and partly to give scientists standard names for quantities like the mass of an electron, about 0.9 rontograms.

Several conventions cause repeated trouble. Symbols above kilo are capitalised, M, G, T, P, E, Z, Y, R, Q, while those from kilo downward are lower case, k, h, da, d, c, m, and so on. This makes case significant: mV is millivolts, MV is megavolts, a factor of a billion apart. Prefixes must not be compounded, so a millionth of a metre is a micrometre, never a millimillimetre, and one nanometre, not one millimicron. A prefixed unit is raised to a power as a whole, so one square kilometre is a million square metres and one cubic centimetre is a millionth of a cubic metre, a fact that trips up volume calculations constantly.

The kilogram is anomalous because it is the only base unit whose name already contains a prefix, an accident of history. Prefixes are therefore applied to the gram, not the kilogram: a millionth of a kilogram is a milligram, and megagram is the formally correct name for what is usually called a tonne.

Finally, computing has its own binary prefixes, standardised as IEC 60027-2 in 1998, in which kibi means 2 to the tenth, or 1024, mebi 2 to the twentieth and gibi 2 to the thirtieth. The historical misuse of kilo, mega and giga for these binary values is the reason a disk sold as one terabyte, meaning ten to the twelve bytes, shows as about 931 gibibytes in an operating system that labels them gigabytes. The bytes are all there; the labels disagree.

sections.heading: Writing the SI correctly: the rules of style
sections.body:
The SI Brochure, published by the BIPM and now in its ninth edition of 2019, specifies not only the units but how to write them, and these rules exist to eliminate ambiguity rather than to enforce fussiness. They are frequently broken in ways that create real errors.

Unit symbols are printed in upright roman type regardless of the surrounding typeface, which distinguishes them from italic quantity symbols. In the expression m equals 5 kg, the italic m is a quantity and the roman kg is a unit. Symbols are never pluralised, so 5 kg not 5 kgs, and never take a full stop except at the end of a sentence, so 5 kg not 5 kg. Symbols are lower case unless the unit is named after a person, in which case the first letter is capitalised: s for second, m for metre, but K for kelvin after Lord Kelvin, A for ampere after Ampère, Pa for pascal, Hz for hertz. The litre is a permitted exception, allowing either l or L because a lower-case l is easily confused with the digit one.

When a unit name is spelled out in full it is written entirely in lower case even if derived from a person's name: one writes ten newtons, a temperature of 300 kelvin, a power of five watts. The single exception is degree Celsius, where the C stays capital. Spelled-out names do take plurals: five metres, ten seconds.

A space always separates the numerical value from the unit symbol, including for the percent sign in the recommended style, with the exception of the degree, minute and second of plane angle, which are set close: 25 °C but 25°. Note that this means the degree symbol and the C are written together with a space before them, not as 25° C. For compound units formed by multiplication, use a space or a centred dot, as in N m or N·m; for division use a solidus or a negative exponent, as in m/s or m s to the minus one, but never more than one solidus in an expression, so write m/s² or m s to the minus two, never m/s/s.

Numbers themselves have conventions. Either the comma or the point may serve as the decimal marker, since practice differs by country, but for that reason neither may be used to group digits. Digits are grouped in threes separated by a thin space: 1 234 567.89 or 1 234 567,89. A number less than one takes a leading zero. Ranges and tolerances must carry the unit on both parts: 20 °C to 25 °C, and 100 mm plus or minus 2 mm, not 100 plus or minus 2 mm if ambiguity could arise. Finally, mixing symbols and names is wrong: write kilometres per hour or km/h, never km per hour.

sections.heading: Realisation and traceability: from the definition to your bathroom scale
sections.body:
A definition written in a brochure weighs nothing on its own. What makes the SI function is an institutional and technical chain connecting that definition to every measuring instrument in use, and that chain has a name: metrological traceability, defined as the property of a measurement result whereby it can be related to a stated reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations, each contributing to the measurement uncertainty.

Three terms are worth distinguishing. A definition states what the unit is. A realisation is a physical experiment that produces the unit from the definition, such as a caesium fountain for the second or a Kibble balance for the kilogram. A dissemination is the process of transferring that realisation down to working instruments through a series of calibrations. Crucially, since 2019 the definitions no longer specify how to realise them, which is a deliberate liberation: the BIPM publishes separate mises en pratique, documents describing currently recommended methods, and any laboratory may use any method that achieves the required uncertainty. When a better technique appears, the practice changes and the definition does not.

The institutional architecture has three tiers. At the top the BIPM at Sèvres coordinates international comparisons and maintains reference time scales. Beneath it sit national metrology institutes: NIST in the United States, NPL in the United Kingdom, PTB in Germany, NIM in China, NRC in Canada and roughly a hundred others, which realise the units nationally and maintain primary standards. Since 1999 these institutes have participated in the CIPM Mutual Recognition Arrangement, under which key comparisons demonstrate equivalence between national standards and calibration certificates issued in one country are accepted in others, a quietly important piece of trade infrastructure.

Below the national institutes sit accredited calibration laboratories, operating to the standard ISO/IEC 17025 and audited by national accreditation bodies, which calibrate instruments for industry. Beneath them are in-house calibration functions in factories and hospitals, and at the bottom the working instrument: the pressure gauge, the pipette, the radiotherapy dosimeter, the fuel dispenser at a filling station.

Each link in the chain adds uncertainty, and each must be documented with a calibration certificate stating the result, its uncertainty and the reference used. An instrument with no traceable calibration is not merely less accurate; strictly, its readings are not measurements in the metrological sense, because there is no defensible statement about what they mean. This is why regulated fields, including legal metrology for trade, clinical laboratories, aviation, pharmaceuticals and nuclear power, mandate traceability explicitly.

The chain also explains the accuracy ladder. A caesium fountain realises the second to about one part in ten to the sixteen, a national frequency standard disseminates to perhaps ten to the thirteen, a rubidium standard in a base station holds ten to the eleven, and a quartz watch keeps ten to the six. Each step loses several orders of magnitude, and that is the normal and expected structure, not a failure. The point of the ladder is that even the watch is connected, in principle, to the caesium atom.

sections.heading: Uncertainty, and what exact really means
sections.body:
The 2019 revision produced a widely misunderstood consequence: several fundamental constants now have zero uncertainty, while others acquired uncertainty they did not previously have. Understanding this requires being clear about what an uncertainty statement is.

Every measurement result is incomplete without a quantitative statement of doubt. The internationally agreed framework is the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement, always called the GUM, first published in 1993 and maintained by a joint committee including the BIPM and ISO. It classifies uncertainty contributions by how they are evaluated, not by their nature. Type A evaluations use statistical analysis of repeated observations, typically the standard deviation of the mean of a series. Type B evaluations use any other means: manufacturer specifications, calibration certificates, published data, physical reasoning about the limits of an effect. The older language of random and systematic error was abandoned because a systematic effect in one measurement becomes a random one when averaged over many laboratories, so the distinction was not stable.

Individual contributions are converted to standard uncertainties, combined by the root-sum-square rule when independent, and the result is a combined standard uncertainty. Because a standard uncertainty corresponds to roughly a sixty-eight percent coverage interval for a normal distribution, results are usually reported as an expanded uncertainty, the combined value multiplied by a coverage factor k, almost always two, giving approximately ninety-five percent coverage. A certificate reading 100.02 mm with expanded uncertainty 0.03 mm and k equal to two means the value is very probably within 99.99 to 100.05 mm.

Against this background, the defining constants are exact in a specific and non-mystical sense: their values are definitions, not measurements, so no experiment can revise them and no uncertainty attaches. The speed of light, the Planck constant, the elementary charge, the Boltzmann constant, the Avogadro constant, the caesium frequency and the luminous efficacy at 540 terahertz all now have exactly zero relative uncertainty. So do quantities derived purely from them, such as the Josephson and von Klitzing constants.

The uncertainty did not vanish; it moved. Quantities that were formerly exact by definition are now measured. The vacuum magnetic permeability, once exactly four pi times ten to the minus seven, now carries a relative uncertainty of about 1.6 parts in ten to the ten, inherited from the fine-structure constant. The molar mass of carbon-12, once exactly twelve grams per mole, is now measured. The mass of the international prototype kilogram, once exactly one kilogram, is now an ordinary object with a measured mass of about one kilogram plus or minus ten micrograms. Nothing became less certain in absolute terms; the bookkeeping simply relocated the uncertainty from where it was inconvenient to where it does no harm.

sections.heading: Failure modes: unit errors, legacy units and how things go wrong
sections.body:
Unit systems fail in practice not through defects in the definitions but through human and organisational error, and the failures are instructive because they are so consistent in shape.

The canonical case is the Mars Climate Orbiter, lost on 23 September 1999 after a 193-day cruise. Ground software supplied by one contractor produced thruster impulse values in pound-force seconds, while the navigation software expected newton seconds, a factor of about 4.45. The discrepancy accumulated over months of small trajectory corrections until the spacecraft entered the Martian atmosphere at roughly 57 kilometres altitude instead of the planned 226 and was destroyed, at a mission cost of about 327 million dollars. The subsequent review found that the error was detectable in the data and that engineers had noticed anomalies but that no process forced the discrepancy to resolution. The lesson is not that anyone was ignorant of units but that an interface between two systems was specified without units being enforced.

The Gimli Glider is the same failure with a happier outcome. On 23 July 1983, Air Canada Flight 143, a Boeing 767, was fuelled using a conversion factor of 1.77 pounds per litre instead of 0.803 kilograms per litre during Canada's transition to metric units, receiving less than half the intended fuel. Both engines flamed out at 41 000 feet and the crew glided the aircraft to a landing at a former air base at Gimli, Manitoba, with no fatalities. Medicine sees smaller versions constantly: milligrams confused with millilitres, micrograms with milligrams, a thousandfold error that is regularly fatal, which is why the abbreviation for microgram is written out in full in many prescribing standards.

Several legacy and non-SI units persist for good reasons and are formally accepted for use with the SI. Time keeps the minute, hour and day. Plane angle keeps the degree, minute and second. Also accepted are the hectare for land area, the litre, the tonne, the astronomical unit, the electronvolt, the dalton, the neper and the bel with its ubiquitous decibel. Deprecated but common are the calorie, the bar, the atmosphere, the torr, the curie, the rad and the rem. Radiation units deserve particular care because the modern gray and sievert are one hundred times the old rad and rem, so an unnoticed substitution produces a hundredfold dose error.

Practical defences are unglamorous and effective. Always carry units through a calculation symbolically and check that the result has the right dimensions, since dimensional analysis catches a large fraction of algebraic errors for free. Convert to coherent base SI units before computing, and remember that prefixed units break coherence. State units explicitly in every interface specification, database column, file format and function signature, and prefer types that carry units where the language allows. Sanity-check magnitudes against something known: a person is about 1.7 metres and 70 kilograms, a car engine 100 kilowatts, room temperature 293 kelvin. A result three orders of magnitude from expectation is a prefix error until proven otherwise.

guides.title: SI Derived Units and Coherent Combinations
guides.summary: A complete reference to the SI derived units: how they are built from the seven base units, what coherence means, the twenty-two named units and the quantities they measure, prefixes and writing rules, dimensional analysis, and the unit errors that have destroyed spacecraft and patients.

sections.heading: Why a System of Derived Units Exists
sections.body:
Measurement only becomes knowledge when the numbers attached to it mean the same thing to everyone who
reads them. A carpenter measuring a beam, a pharmacist compounding a dose, and a satellite navigation
receiver computing a position are all doing the same act: comparing some physical quantity against an
agreed reference and reporting the ratio. The International System of Units, abbreviated SI from the
French Systeme International d'Unites, is the modern global agreement about what those references are.
It was formally adopted in 1960 by the eleventh General Conference on Weights and Measures, the treaty
body established by the Metre Convention of 1875, and it is now the legal basis of measurement in
essentially every country on Earth, including the United States, whose customary inch and pound have
been defined by exact reference to the metre and kilogram since 1959.

The system rests on a small number of base units, and then on a much larger family of derived units
built from them by multiplication and division alone. That second half is where most practical
measurement actually lives. Almost nothing anyone measures in daily life is a base quantity. Speed is
length divided by time. Force is mass times acceleration. Pressure is force spread over area. Electrical
resistance is voltage divided by current, and voltage is itself power divided by current. Each of these
is a derived quantity, and each has a derived unit whose definition follows from the physics rather than
from any separate act of legislation.

This is not merely bookkeeping. Because derived units are built by pure multiplication and division
without arbitrary numerical factors, the equations of physics can be written without conversion
constants cluttering them. In SI, work equals force times distance, full stop: one joule is one newton
acting through one metre, with no factor of 32.174 or 778 or 4.186 in the way. Older systems were not
like this. The foot-pound-second world needed the poundal and the slug and a gravitational constant
sprinkled through its formulae; the calorie and the British thermal unit sat awkwardly beside mechanical
energy units, so that converting heat into work required a remembered number, the mechanical equivalent
of heat, which James Prescott Joule spent years measuring in the 1840s. SI removes that whole class of
error by construction.

The practical payoff is that a unit expression carries an audit trail. If a calculation produces an
answer in kilograms per second squared when the quantity ought to be an energy, the units themselves
announce that something has gone wrong, usually long before a plausible-looking but wrong number reaches
anyone who might act on it. Learning to read units as algebra, not as decoration appended to a numeral,
is one of the highest-leverage habits available to anyone who works quantitatively, and it costs nothing
but attention.

sections.heading: The Seven Base Units and the 2019 Redefinition
sections.body:
Everything in SI is generated from seven base units: the second for time, the metre for length, the
kilogram for mass, the ampere for electric current, the kelvin for thermodynamic temperature, the mole
for amount of substance, and the candela for luminous intensity. The choice of exactly these seven is
partly historical and partly conventional. There is no deep law of nature requiring seven; one could in
principle build a consistent system with fewer, and theoretical physicists routinely work in systems
where the speed of light and Planck's constant are set to one and lengths, times and masses all collapse
into a single dimension. The seven were chosen because they span the practical measurement needs of
science, industry and commerce with a manageable number of independent standards to maintain.

On 20 May 2019 the definitions of four of these units changed profoundly, and the change is worth
understanding because it explains why modern unit definitions look so strange at first reading. Before
that date, the kilogram was defined by a single platinum-iridium cylinder kept in a vault at Sevres near
Paris, the International Prototype of the Kilogram. That artefact had, by comparison with its official
copies, apparently drifted by roughly 50 micrograms over a century, and nobody could say with certainty
whether the prototype had lost mass or the copies had gained it, because by definition the prototype was
exactly one kilogram whatever it happened to weigh. This is an unacceptable foundation.

The 2019 revision fixed the numerical values of seven defining constants exactly and let the units fall
out of them. The second is defined by fixing the caesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency at exactly
9 192 631 770 hertz. The metre follows by fixing the speed of light at exactly 299 792 458 metres per
second, so that a metre is the distance light travels in 1/299 792 458 of a second. The kilogram is now
defined by fixing the Planck constant at exactly 6.626 070 15 times ten to the minus thirty-four joule
seconds, realised in practice with a Kibble balance, an instrument that weighs a mass against an
electromagnetic force whose strength is known in quantum electrical terms. The ampere is fixed through
the elementary charge at exactly 1.602 176 634 times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs; the kelvin
through the Boltzmann constant at exactly 1.380 649 times ten to the minus twenty-three joules per
kelvin; the mole through the Avogadro number at exactly 6.022 140 76 times ten to the twenty-third per
mole; and the candela through a fixed luminous efficacy of 683 lumens per watt at a frequency of 540
terahertz.

The consequence is that SI is no longer anchored to any object. Any laboratory anywhere, now or in ten
thousand years, can in principle reconstruct every unit from physics alone, and the definitions cannot
drift because the constants are defined rather than measured.

sections.heading: What Coherence Actually Means
sections.body:
The word coherent has a precise technical meaning in metrology that is easy to skip over and important
to grasp. A derived unit is coherent when it is formed from base units purely as a product of powers,
with a numerical factor of exactly one. The metre per second is coherent: one metre per second is one
metre divided by one second, with no multiplier. The kilometre per hour is not coherent, because
converting it into base units introduces the factor 1000/3600, which is 0.2777 and so on. Both are
perfectly legitimate units, and the kilometre per hour is far more convenient on a road sign, but only
the coherent one slots into equations without carrying a conversion constant along with it.

The practical importance of coherence is that it guarantees a closure property. If every quantity in a
calculation is expressed in coherent SI units, the result is automatically in the coherent SI unit for
whatever quantity emerges, with no numerical adjustment anywhere. Feed a force in newtons and a distance
in metres into the definition of work and the answer is in joules, exactly. Feed a mass in kilograms and
a velocity in metres per second into one-half m v squared and the answer is again in joules, exactly,
with no need to remember whether kinetic energy and work happen to share a scale factor. They share it
because the system was constructed so that they must.

This is precisely what earlier systems lacked. In the engineering foot-pound-second system, force in
pounds-force and mass in pounds-mass differ by the factor g sub c, approximately 32.174, and generations
of students have lost marks and engineers have lost hardware to its misplacement. In the centimetre-gram-
second electromagnetic systems there were competing coherent sets, Gaussian and electrostatic and
electromagnetic, each internally consistent but mutually incompatible, and factors of four pi appeared
or vanished in Maxwell's equations depending on which one you had chosen. SI rationalised
electromagnetism by absorbing the four pi into the definitions of the electric and magnetic constants,
which is why the SI form of Coulomb's law carries a one over four pi epsilon-nought that the Gaussian
form does not.

Coherence has one deliberate exception baked into the system, and it is a famous irritation. The
coherent unit of mass is the kilogram, which already carries a prefix. Every other base unit is
prefix-free. This is a historical accident: the original unit was the gramme, defined in 1795, but the
practical standard manufactured in 1799 was a kilogram-sized artefact, and the artefact won. The
consequence is that when you form prefixes on mass you attach them to the gram, not the kilogram, so
that a millionth of a kilogram is a milligram and never a microkilogram. Everything else in the system
is more regular than this one blemish suggests.

sections.heading: Dimensional Analysis: The Algebra of Units
sections.body:
Behind every unit sits a dimension, and the two are not the same thing. A dimension is the kind of
quantity being measured; a unit is a particular reference amount of it. Length is a dimension, written
L; the metre and the light-year are two units of it. SI recognises seven independent dimensions matching
its seven base units, written L for length, M for mass, T for time, I for current, capital theta for
temperature, N for amount of substance and J for luminous intensity. Every physical quantity has a dimensional formula that is a product of powers of
these, independent of which units anyone chooses.

Velocity has dimensions L T to the minus one. Acceleration is L T to the minus two. Force, by Newton's
second law, is mass times acceleration, so M L T to the minus two. Energy is force times distance, so
M L squared T to the minus two. Power is energy per time, M L squared T to the minus three. Pressure is
force per area, M L to the minus one T to the minus two. These formulae let you check any equation
mechanically. The principle of dimensional homogeneity states that every additive term in a physically
meaningful equation must carry the same dimensions, and that you can never add a length to a time or a
pressure to an energy. If a derivation produces such a sum, the derivation is wrong, and you have found
the error without checking a single number.

Dimensional analysis does more than catch mistakes; it can generate physics. The classic demonstration
is Geoffrey Ingram Taylor's 1950 estimate of the yield of the first atomic test. Taylor reasoned that
the radius R of a blast wave could depend only on the energy released E, the density of the surrounding
air rho, and the elapsed time t. The only dimensionally consistent combination is R proportional to the
one-fifth power of E t squared over rho. Given published photographs with a scale bar and timing marks,
he read off a yield of about twenty kilotons, which was then classified information. The same method
gives the period of a pendulum as proportional to the square root of length over gravity, without
solving any differential equation.

The formal statement of this power is the Buckingham pi theorem, published by Edgar Buckingham in 1914.
It says that a physical relationship among n variables involving k independent dimensions can be
rewritten as a relationship among exactly n minus k dimensionless groups. Those groups are the
Reynolds number, the Mach number, the Froude number and their kin, and they are why a scale model in a
wind tunnel can predict the behaviour of a full-size aircraft.

The limit of the method is that it is blind to dimensionless constants: it will tell you that a
quantity must scale as the square root of something, but never whether the coefficient is one, one-half
or two pi. It also fails if you have omitted a relevant variable, and it cannot distinguish quantities
that share a dimensional formula, such as torque and energy.

sections.heading: The Twenty-Two Named Derived Units
sections.body:
Most derived units have no special name and are simply written as combinations: metres per second,
kilograms per cubic metre, ampere-hours turned into coulombs. But twenty-two derived units carry names
of their own, granted because the combinations they represent occur so often that writing them out in
base units every time would be intolerable. Each name is a shorthand, exactly equal to its base-unit
expression, and each may be freely substituted for it.

The list, with the quantity each measures, runs as follows. The radian and steradian measure plane and
solid angle and are dimensionless ratios. The hertz measures frequency and equals one per second. The
newton measures force, equal to a kilogram metre per second squared. The pascal measures pressure and
stress, one newton per square metre. The joule measures energy, work and heat, one newton metre. The
watt measures power and radiant flux, one joule per second. The coulomb measures electric charge, one
ampere second. The volt measures electric potential difference, one watt per ampere. The farad measures
capacitance, one coulomb per volt. The ohm measures electrical resistance, one volt per ampere. The
siemens measures electrical conductance and is the reciprocal ohm. The weber measures magnetic flux, one
volt second. The tesla measures magnetic flux density, one weber per square metre. The henry measures
inductance, one weber per ampere. The degree Celsius measures Celsius temperature and is exactly the
same size as the kelvin, offset by 273.15. The lumen measures luminous flux, one candela steradian. The
lux measures illuminance, one lumen per square metre. The becquerel measures radioactive activity, one
decay per second. The gray measures absorbed radiation dose, one joule per kilogram. The sievert
measures equivalent and effective dose, also dimensionally one joule per kilogram. And the katal
measures catalytic activity, one mole per second, the newest addition, adopted in 1999.

The naming convention deserves care because it is a common source of sloppy writing. When a unit is
named after a person, the unit name itself is written in lower case in running text, but its symbol is
capitalised. So one writes ten newtons, not ten Newtons, but the symbol is N. Likewise pascal and Pa,
watt and W, kelvin and K, hertz and Hz. Units not named after people take lower-case symbols: metre and
m, second and s, mole and mol. The litre is a special case, permitted as either l or L because a
lower-case l is easily confused with the digit one.

Notice how many of these names cluster in electromagnetism. That is not coincidence. Mechanics needs
only a handful because its quantities are simple products of length, mass and time, whereas electrical
quantities involve current in various powers and their base-unit expressions become grotesque. The ohm
written out in full is kilogram metre squared per second cubed per ampere squared, which nobody could
read at a glance, and that unreadability is precisely the argument for the name.

sections.heading: Mechanical Units: Newton, Pascal, Joule and Watt
sections.body:
The four workhorse mechanical units form a chain, each defined from the one before, and understanding
the chain makes each of them intuitive rather than memorised. The newton is the force that gives a
one-kilogram mass an acceleration of one metre per second squared. It is a small unit by everyday
standards: the weight of a medium apple at Earth's surface is roughly one newton, and an average adult
of seventy kilograms weighs about 687 newtons, since the standard acceleration due to gravity is
9.806 65 metres per second squared by definition. That defined value, adopted in 1901, is a convention
rather than a measurement, since actual local gravity varies from about 9.780 at the equator to 9.832 at
the poles, a spread of about half a percent that matters in precision weighing.

The pascal is one newton spread over one square metre, and it is a very small pressure. Standard
atmospheric pressure is 101 325 pascals, so meteorologists use the hectopascal, exactly equal to the
older millibar, and quote sea-level pressure around 1013 hPa. Car tyres run near 220 kilopascals
absolute, or about 32 pounds per square inch gauge. Blood pressure stubbornly remains in millimetres of
mercury, where 120 mmHg is about 16 kilopascals, and this is one of the few places where a non-SI unit
survives in serious clinical use because the entire diagnostic literature is calibrated in it.

The joule is one newton acting through one metre. It is likewise small: lifting a one-kilogram book one
metre takes about 9.8 joules. A dietary Calorie, capitalised, is a kilocalorie, equal to 4184 joules, so
a 2000 Calorie daily intake is about 8.4 megajoules. The joule also measures heat, and the fact that a
single unit serves for mechanical work, heat and electrical energy is the whole content of the first law
of thermodynamics made visible in the unit system. One kilowatt hour, the unit on an electricity bill,
is 3.6 megajoules exactly.

The watt is one joule per second. A human at rest dissipates about 100 watts, a brisk cyclist sustains
perhaps 200 to 250 watts, and a fit athlete can hold 400 watts for an hour. An electric kettle draws
2 to 3 kilowatts. Horsepower, still common in vehicle specifications, comes in two flavours: mechanical
horsepower at 745.7 watts and metric horsepower at 735.5 watts, and the difference of one and a half
percent is enough to matter in a specification dispute.

Two mechanical quantities are worth flagging for their subtlety. Torque has the same dimensions as
energy and could be written in joules, but by convention is always written newton metres to signal that
it is not energy and that adding it to an energy would be meaningless. And frequency in hertz shares
